articles.title: Political Influencers as Information Sources: Experimental Evidence on Credibility, Belief, and Epistemic Judgment
articles.abstract: Political influencers are increasingly important sources of political information on social media, yet how citizens evaluate information attributed to them remains understudied. Using a survey experiment in Canada, we compare how citizens evaluate identical political statements when attributed to influencers, national news, or no source. We examine perceived credibility, belief, and judgment accuracy. Results show that influencer attribution lowers perceived credibility and reduces confidence in accurate political information compared with national news, although these differences vary by ideological orientation. Followers initially report greater belief in false political claims attributed to influencers than recognizers, but this difference weakens substantially after accounting for observed differences between the groups. These findings suggest that influencers’ impact as political information sources depends on both audience characteristics and selection into influencer audiences, underscoring the distinction between audience reach and epistemic authority in hybrid media systems.

articles.title: Exploring Nonlinear Associations Between AI Comment Volume and Retail Investor Sentiment
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence comment generators have proliferated in online stock forums. However, how AI comment volume associates with retail investor sentiment, and whether this association is conditional on market volatility and annual AI comment density, remain under- explored. Using weekly data from the East Money Stock Forum and the Shanghai Composite Index spanning May 2019–October 2024 in China, this paper proposed a two-detector ensemble for AI comment detection, then investigated nonlinear associations between AI comment volume and retail investor sentiment under three tiers of market volatility and six annual AI comment densities. Our generalized additive model (GAM) results show that AI comment volume exhibits a weak, net-positive nonlinear association with mean retail investor sentiment, and a very weak net-negative nonlinear association with sentiment divergence. We find no statistically significant pairwise differences in these associations across low-, medium- and high-volatility levels. For annual AI comment density, statistically significant cross-density differences are observed for sentiment standard deviation in multiple year pairwise comparisons, whereas only one comparison yields significant differences for mean sentiment. Collectively, our findings indicate that merely considering the number of AI comments provides limited information regarding the sentiment of retail investors.

articles.title: Why Anthropology Needs Biocultural Ethnography
articles.abstract: Many cultural anthropologists have long been skeptical of collaboration with the other subfields of the discipline at large—in particular, biological or evolutionary anthropology—for fear of treading over long-settled ground regarding the problematic roots of anthropology in which the so-called “evolutionists” and social Darwinists promoted pseudoscience in an attempt to legitimize a range of bigoted and ethnocentric assumptions about humanity. In many anthropology departments, the entire research faculty is comprised solely of cultural anthropologists who neither think of themselves as scientists nor of their field as scientific. This is to anthropology’s detriment, as it needlessly limits not only the scope of discovery anthropologists can make, even in fieldwork, but it also reframes anthropology departments and their associated research projects within the scope of federal funding as strictly social science and humanities initiatives, putting them in financial and academic jeopardy. While it is certainly true that anthropology has a problematic history intertwined with pseudoscience, this does not justify a conscious initiative to rhetorically and conceptually divorce real science from cultural anthropology. In this chapter, the authors demonstrate through their own prior works across both theory and practice the tangible benefits and essential breakthroughs of approaching cultural anthropology and ethnographic fieldwork, when applicable, via biocultural frameworks that take holistic and ontological considerations of field sites, persons, and cultural modalities into account. The authors argue that by embracing the entirety of anthropology as a science, rather than shying away from this fact, the design and nuance of many more ethnographic projects—and their subsequent findings and insights about the human condition—stand to be greatly enriched.

articles.title: Commenting at the Water's Edge: Party Brands and Expressed Partisanship on Ukraine Aid, 2022–2024
articles.abstract: Party brand theory holds that voters attach more strongly to parties they can tell apart, and it has tested that claim by asking them. We ask instead what they wrote. Across 34 months of r/politics discussion of Ukraine aid from March 2022 to December 2024, we annotated 217,494 comments with a five-task language model annotation suite measuring whether a comment is recognizable as partisan, which coalition's discourse it resembles, and three components of partisan social identity. We regressed the resulting monthly series on the Party Brand Index of Shi et al. (2026), estimated from contemporaneous news coverage, using HAC standard errors and a whole-submission bootstrap. Clearer party brands accompanied more recognizable and stronger partisan expression: a ten-point difference in the Party Brand Index corresponded to a .060 difference in monthly mean Affiliation Recognizability and a .0067 difference in Conditional PSI. Roughly seven tenths of the combined association sit in how many comments were recognizably partisan and three tenths in how strongly they expressed it, while the particular expressive form of the average association remained unresolved. Clearer party brands were therefore accompanied more by partisanship becoming visible than by partisanship becoming intense, aligning with the classic survey findings from the party brand theory. Months in which either party was represented as more opposed to aid were months in which the monthly discourse leaned more toward the Democratic coalition, and the within-month gap in expressed strength between the two coalitions widened as brands clarified.

articles.title: Constructing Adversaries: Strategic Narratives in U.S. State Department Press Briefings Corpus on Russia and China (2001–2024)
articles.abstract: In recent decades, Russia and China have emerged as the United States’ major strategic competitors, whereas Washington perceives both as “revisionist powers”. The growing literature focuses on Russia’s and China’s rival narratives in the global community, while treating U.S. foreign policy discourses as a reactive backdrop. To address this scarcity, the study compares U.S. foreign policy narratives toward Russia and China, asking how U.S. diplomatic narratives associate Russia and China with different foreign policy issues over a long timeframe. Adopting computational methods and statistical modeling to analyze 12,129 pairs of questions and answers from U.S. State Department Press Briefings from 2001 to 2024, this study captures how foreign policy narratives toward its rivals were structured, differentiated, and sustained across four presidencies. The results provide a systematic analysis of the institutionalized yet nuanced differences in the American foreign policy narrative toward its biggest strategic rivals over nearly 25 years of geopolitical dynamics, demonstrating that U.S. official diplomatic narratives are constrained by both geopolitical dynamism in foreign-policy issue attention and institutional patterns in issue association, while presidential administrations are relegated to a secondary role. The study contributes to the constructivist approach to international relations, foreign policy issue attention, and strategic narrative theory.

articles.title: The Ties that Bind: Growing Up with Immigrants and Later Life Attitudes toward Immigration
articles.authors: Justin Robinson, Pavlos Vasilopoulos, Haley McAvay
articles.abstract: In recent years, inequalities in residential environments have received much attention as an explanation for the appeal of anti-immigration parties across advanced democracies. This paper explores the long-term association between neighborhood and school context in adolescence and attitudes towards immigration later in life, drawing on a UK-based cohort study matched with fine-grained census data on immigrant composition across both sites of contact. Drawing on the premises of the impressionable years hypothesis, neighbourhood effects, and contact theory, we posit that as a space of social interaction and socialisation, the presence of immigrants in the local area that one experiences in adolescence is influential to the development of positive immigration attitudes in adulthood. Our findings suggest that the share of immigrants in one’s neighbourhood and school during adolescence has a persistent positive association with favorable attitudes toward immigration among White British respondents 18 years later, net of parental characteristics in adolescence and individual and residential characteristics in adulthood. Further, this positive effect is robust in an instrumental variable design using an immigrant enclave shift-share instrument. These findings highlight the role of early-years socialization experiences in the formation of out-group attitudes and the importance of inter-group contact for fostering tolerant societies.

articles.title: Quantifying the Carbon Preserved by Protected Areas in the Amazon
articles.authors: Rafael Araujo, Arthur Bragança, Francisco Costa, Marcelo Sant'Anna, Eduardo Adame, Frank Gentile

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Protected areas (PAs) are among the most important instruments for curbing emissions from deforestation in the Amazon, yet their effectiveness remains debated. In this paper, we evaluate the forest cover and carbon each PA preserves in the Amazon biome. We use an economic land-use model estimated from satellite-based biomass and land-use data. We find that PAs prevent the deforestation of 394,763 km2 and avoid releasing 5.68 billion tCO2 of carbon stored in standing forest---about 16% of global yearly emissions. Three-quarters of the avoided emissions stem from forests that would otherwise have been converted to pasture. Effectiveness varies with accessibility and agricultural potential: PAs closer to markets and with high pasture suitability avert twice as much carbon loss as remote PAs. These results quantify the carbon value of protection and highlight where conservation yields the highest climate gains.

articles.title: The Local and the Firm: Divergent Immigration Outcomes in Brazil
articles.abstract: How can adverse formal-sector effects of immigration at the regional level coexist with favorable outcomes inside the establishments that hire immigrants? We use matched employer-employee data from Brazil for 2000 to 2017 to estimate regional effects and characterize establishment-level patterns. We instrument regional immigrant exposure with a shift-share design that combines past immigrant settlements with country-of-origin inflows predicted by push factors such as environmental disasters and political instability. Greater exposure reduces the number of establishments hiring formally, lowers native formal wages, and increases native layoffs. Yet establishments employ more native workers and pay slightly higher native earnings after their first immigrant hire. These establishment-level estimates are descriptive because immigrant hiring is endogenous. The contrast shows that outcomes within immigrant-hiring establishments do not capture immigration's full incidence across a local labor market, consistent with adjustment across establishments or between formal and informal employment.

articles.title: Beyond the Lockdown: Long-Term Impact of COVID-19 on Registered Domestic Violence in the Netherlands
articles.authors: Junia Bergers, Anne Coomans, Sjoukje van Deuren, Steve van de Weijer, Arjan Blokland, veroni eichelsheim
articles.abstract: Domestic violence is a pervasive, societal issue impacting millions of people worldwide. While numerous studies have examined the short-term impact of the COVID-19 restrictions on domestic violence, research on its long-term effects remains limited. This study aims to explore the long-term impact of the pandemic on domestic violence trends in the Netherlands. Through descriptive quantitative analyses of official registrations and advisory requests from national domestic violence agencies from March 2019 to March 2024, covering one year before, two years during, and two years after the pandemic, this study investigates potential delayed or catch-up effects in domestic violence registrations using descriptive analyses. The results show a decline in the number of reports during the pandemic, followed by a rebound in the two years after it ended, reaching levels slightly below pre-pandemic levels. However, shifts in reporting behavior were observed, with a gradual increase in reports by individuals directly involved and a decrease in reports from family members and neighbors. Notably, while official reports suggested no long-term increase in domestic violence registrations, advisory requests continued to increase. These findings highlight discrepancies in data sources and emphasize the need for careful consideration of existing patterns and reporting thresholds when interpreting trends.

articles.title: Provoking Polarization: From Public Antagonism to Private Conflict
articles.abstract: This article develops a cultural sociological account of political polarization as a dynamic and performative process centered on provocation. It introduces a dual framework of performative polarization and micropolarization to explain how public antagonisms and interpersonal conflicts are co-constituted. At the public level, polarization unfolds through provocative performances that stage moral binaries and elicit reactive engagement. At the interpersonal level, these antagonisms are taken up in everyday interactions, where they are experienced as struggles for recognition shaped by publicly circulating stigma. Provocation is conceptualized as the key mechanism linking these levels: by generating affective responses and visible opposition, it amplifies public conflict while providing emotionally charged scripts that are reproduced in private relationships. Drawing on qualitative interviews conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic in Germany, the article illustrates how public provocations reverberate within intimate settings. The analysis highlights the affective, relational, and microsociological foundations of contemporary polarization.

articles.title: Love, Loathing, and Loyalty: Affective Publics and Antagonism in TikTok Comments Sections
articles.authors: Matthias Revers, Julia Niemann-Lenz, Lasse Rodeck, Hendrik Meyer
articles.abstract: This study examines TikTok video content and comment sections during the 2025 German federal election campaign. We conceptualize comment sections as affective publics: networked arenas in which users enact publicness through affirmation, opposition, and emotional expression. Empirically, the analysis draws on 12,685 videos from 1,274 political accounts, engagement metrics, and almost two million comments, examined through LLM-based topic classification and automated stance and emotion classification. Methodologically, the study shows how LLM-assisted analysis can move beyond content classification to trace how political messages are taken up, emotionally charged, and redirected in audience interaction. Results show that campaign-focused content dominates political TikTok, followed by more substantive debate about economic issues, democracy and its institutions, social policy, and migration. Yet visibility of this content and audience responses vary sharply across parties. The AfD combines high posting frequency with strongly supportive and emotionally aligned comment environments, while centrist and governing parties face predominantly critical or mocking responses. Cross-party hostility analysis further reveals asymmetric patterns of animosity, with negative engagement directed toward specific political opponents rather than distributed randomly. The study shows that TikTok functions simultaneously as a space of participatory visibility and affective polarization. Conceptually, it extends the study of affective publics to platformed campaign communication, showing how emotional alignment and antagonism organize visibility and engagement on TikTok.

articles.title: Reassessing the Democratic Advantage in War

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Democratic initiators are widely held to win interstate wars far more often than autocracies. Yet this ``democratic advantage'' rests on one war dataset, the Correlates of War (COW), and a few democracy measures. We reassess it using 11 operationalizations of democracy and Project Mars, a far larger dataset of wars. Across 490 estimates, we find no robust advantage for democratic initiators. With standard controls, Project Mars contrasts between democratic and non-democratic initiators range from -12 to +8 percentage points; none is significant. A 1,408-specification multiverse shows the advantage fades as controls are added: only 5.8\% of Project Mars specifications are significant, and the Bayesian model average (11 points) is indistinguishable from zero. Project Mars rules out advantages of 15 points or more; COW, by contrast, has too few democratic initiators to settle the question. Research that treats democracies as the benchmark of wartime success may rest on a baseline that does not exist.

articles.title: Degrowth and Biodiversity
articles.abstract: Biodiversity conservation is an uphill struggle against the pressures of an economic system with a structural need to expand. Furthermore, there are reasons to question that economic growth contributes to human welfare beyond a certain point, and also that it can be sustained for much longer, due to ecological and social limits. Proponents of degrowth seek to transition to an economy that no longer needs to grow, in ways that are nontraumatic, democratic and equitable, envisaging a society where the priority is to fulfill everybody’s physical and emotional needs without compromising the integrity of what remains of the biosphere.

articles.title: The Possibility of Inclusive Public Religion: Revisiting the Deliberative-Consensual Model
articles.abstract: Can the deliberative-consensual model foster inclusive public religion, or does its apparent success depend on illiberal interventions and social power relations that liberal theory fails to acknowledge? Addressing critiques of the liberal public sphere, this article examines the conditions under which religiously motivated organizations can contribute to pluralistic public life. It compares two Islamic civil society organizations in Turkey: the Emek ve Adalet Platformu (EAP), which promotes cross-ideological cooperation and social justice, and the Furkan Vakfı (FV), which prioritizes unity around a particular interpretation of Islam. Drawing on organizational documents, public discourse, accounts of organizational activities, and participant observation, the analysis first examines whether differences in class, gender, and ethnicity adequately explain the organizations’ divergent approaches to inclusivity. The available evidence does not establish sufficient differences along these dimensions to account for the contrast. Instead, the article identifies two principles derived from Habermasian deliberative theory as key explanatory dimensions: deliberative tolerance, understood as a willingness to engage across religious and ideological boundaries without requiring prior agreement, and a rational-critical debate ethos, understood as openness to questioning, criticism, and the reconsideration of established positions. The EAP exemplifies these principles through its cross-sector collaborations, consultative organizational practices, and public forums that bring diverse perspectives into dialogue. The FV, by contrast, illustrates how extensive public engagement can coexist with restricted pluralistic exchange when religious authority limits the legitimacy of alternative interpretations and independent criticism. The comparison demonstrates that the normative and practical resources of the deliberative-consensual model can help explain the emergence of inclusive public religion without recourse to illiberal interventions. The findings reaffirm the model’s analytical relevance while highlighting the importance of how religious organizations institutionalize openness to difference and critical reasoning. Keywords: public religion; deliberative democracy; Habermas; pluralism; Islamic civil society; Turkey; deliberative tolerance; public sphere

articles.title: Design Document and Clinical Rationale: A Two-Layer AI Digital Readiness Coach for Adolescent Vaping Cessation
articles.authors: Siddharth Dhananjay Kulkarni, Nicholas Glover, Arush Satasiya
articles.abstract: Nicotine vaping among adolescents is of growing concern, especially among those who use nicotine regularly and are not able to quit. School administrators most often respond to a case of vaping by increasing discipline, often leading to the exclusion of the student. However, punitive measures may not address the student's dependence. The goal of this research is to develop a two-layer, adaptable artificial intelligence (AI) digital coach to support adolescent vaping cessation using evidence-based clinical practices. The system employs TTM, MI, and CBT to create conversational strategies to address an individual's readiness to change, momentary motivation, and barriers to change. The system is designed to respond to users' needs based on conversational assessments rather than rigid classifications of stages or behaviors. The server-side routing uses Change Talk and Sustain Talk to respond to users in an engaging, motivational manner, helping them develop a quit plan. Further, the system constructs a barrier profile to determine the presence of nicotine dependence and polysubstance use. If a barrier profile indicates high dependence, the system offers a referral to a school nurse or counselor for further judgment and engagement. The server-side employs risk screening and various safety measures, including localizing the machine-learning model, to mitigate potential harm to the adolescent. The system will be evaluated based on its fidelity to Motivational Interviewing and its ability to promote biochemical abstinence in a randomized, controlled setting.

articles.title: The party politics of European integration: Explaining conditionality and solidarity in times of crisis

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: How does the European Union (EU) manage to deepen integration amid recurring crises? While existing literature on crisis management and resilience in Europe emphasizes institutional mechanisms, it often overlooks the critical role of domestic political coalitions in enabling two-level bargaining during crises. This paper builds a theory of how conditionality and solidarity alternate through crises. It conceptualizes a sequential two-level game approach to the politics of crisis management in the EU. Domestically, pro-European parties strive to balance responsibility towards the EU with promises of benefits at the national level. This takes different forms in Northern and Southern countries. In order to justify cross-country solidarity in the North, federalists need to ensure a certain level of oversight and conditionality on the use of the resources transferred. Such level of oversight acts as a constraint for pro-EU parties in Southern countries, which while endorsing it need to convince their electorate that cooperation will result in higher levels of welfare guaranteed by the EU. This approach offers a way to understand the differentiated trade-offs that pro-European political parties must navigate in different member states. What, then, explains variations in the levels of solidarity between different crises? The second part of my framework suggests that policy paradigms have `diminishing returns', whereby previous crisis management failures constrain future policies. The paper suggests that the temporal dimension of crises succession matters, in as much as previous crisis management can either discourage new acts of solidarity or swing national debates towards social protection, given the diminishing returns of previous policy paradigms and the process of learning through crises. As welfare enhancements promised by European integration fail to be perceived by citizens, anti-Europeanism rises in Southern countries. Conversely, widespread solidarity not compensated by equally evident acts of responsibilization of member states lead to increases in Nordic countries' anti-EU sentiments. This theory is tested through an analysis of parliamentary debates during recent periods of crisis.

articles.title: Sustainable Ageing: Conceptualizing Ageing in a Forward-Looking and Multilevel Perspective
articles.authors: Bruno Arpino, Valeria Bordone, Pearl A. Dykstra
articles.abstract: Population ageing is one of the defining transformations of contemporary societies, yet the question of whether ageing is sustainable is often reduced to fiscal pressure, healthcare demand, or the capacity of individuals to remain healthy and active. We develop sustainable ageing as an integrative conceptual and policy framework that connects individual and population ageing with sustainability concerns. Drawing on gerontology, life-course research, and literature on social-determinants of wellbeing, we specify the added value of sustainable ageing through four features: a forward-looking and intergenerational criterion, a life-course perspective, a multilevel structure, and an explicit treatment of trade-offs among economic, social, health and care, technological, environmental, political-institutional and cultural dimensions. We conceptually distinguish these dimensions (what must be sustained) from the conditions and policy levers through which sustainability may be supported, including education, care arrangements, labour markets, housing, and governance. We then outline a policy agenda that makes institutional responsibility and redistribution explicit. We propose a measurement strategy for future research that would distinguish current outcomes from their sustainability over time and assess the latter in relation to financial feasibility, ecological limits, social minimums, and distributional consequences. Sustainable ageing is best understood not as another label for ageing well, nor as a classification of successful older individuals, but as a framework for evaluating whether ageing trajectories and ageing societies can reproduce the resources and capabilities required for present and future generations to flourish.

articles.title: The Winogradsky Column: A Living Diagram for Designing and Representing Ecosystems
articles.abstract: In recent years, microbiology has undergone a significant shift from the study of isolated organisms to the analysis of microbial assemblages and ecological interactions. Within this context, devices capable of making such relational complexity observable, such as ecological microcosms, have acquired renewed relevance. Among them, the Winogradsky column occupies a distinctive place as a classical experimental system in microbiology. Drawing on semiotics and science and technology studies, this article examines the Winogradsky column as a material-semiotic device, focusing on its capacity to visualize chemical exchanges and biological processes, and to represent and design ecosystems. The argument is grounded in observations conducted at the Giovannelli Laboratory in Naples, where Winogradsky-based microcosms are developed and used, alongside other analytical and experimental techniques, to study microbial communities from extreme environments. The analysis shows that the column operates simultaneously as a visualization device, an experimental system, and a material archive: it makes metabolic processes perceptible through stratified form and chromatic differentiation, allows the manipulation of environmental parameters, and preserves relational assemblages rather than isolated organisms. The article argues that the Winogradsky column can be understood as a “living diagram”, a material-semiotic configuration and experimental device in which visual intelligibility structure emerges from the spatial and chromatic self-organization of living matter. Through this configuration, the column redefines the relationship between laboratory experiment and ecosystem, rendering ecological relations observable while actively reconfiguring them.

articles.title: Wie unterscheiden sich die Berufsaspirationen von Schüler*innen mit sonderpädagogischen Förderbedarfen in verschiedenen institutionellen Rahmenbedingungen am Ende der Sekundarstufe I?
articles.authors: Christoph Homuth, Monja Schmitt, Sebastian Bauer
articles.abstract: More than half of all students with special educational needs (SEN) in Germany are taught ex-clusively at special schools, even though the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Dis-abilities sets inclusive education as a policy goal. Researchers have rarely examined whether inclusive schooling affects occupational aspirations, as national research has focused almost exclusively on comparing special-school students with students without SEN. Drawing on data from the National Educational Panel Study (Starting Cohort 4), this study compares four groups for the first time: special-school students, mainstream students with SEN taught under same-goal curricula, mainstream students with SEN taught under differentiated-goal curricula, and mainstream students without SEN. Because SEN ascription and school placement are non-random and relate to social origin, cognitive abilities, and other traits, we balance the groups on these via entropy balancing. Weighted regression then tests whether aspiration gaps stem from SEN status itself, implying similar disadvantages for special-school and inclusively taught stu-dents with SEN, or from school context, implying that inclusively taught students with SEN fall between special-school students and students without SEN. Results show that inclusively taught students with SEN do not differ in occupational aspirations from students without SEN, regard-less of curriculum type, but report markedly higher aspirations than special-school students. Contrary to expectations, this gap is explained little by social origin or competencies but relates more to the lower average aspiration level of classmates at special schools. The findings con-tribute to inequality research on institutional segregation and provide evidence for expanding in-clusive education.

articles.title: Feeling the Heat: Urban Heat Inequality, Physical Well-Being, and the Social Response to Climate Change
articles.abstract: Research on social responses to climate change often argues that direct experiences of extreme weather can shape public attitudes, policy preferences, and political behaviour. Yet such responses presuppose that individuals experience climatic conditions as meaningful in their everyday lives. This chapter examines whether local exposure to extreme temperatures is associated with reduced physical well-being, a potential mechanism linking climate exposure to broader social and political responses. Combining geocoded data from Understanding Society with high-resolution temperature estimates for London and Birmingham (2009--2017), we link neighbourhood-level heat exposure during the three days preceding the interview to respondents' physical functioning. The results reveal that neighbourhood-level temperature inequalities are associated with health differences -- particularly among women -- but these experiences do not translate into pro-environmental behaviour. Moreover, week associations in individual fixed-effects models suggest that the health consequences of urban heat are closely intertwined with persistent spatial inequalities in exposure and vulnerability.

articles.title: Too old for the job? Two preregistered experiments on age bias in hiring
articles.authors: Adrian F. Rogne, Edvard N. Larsen, Anne Skevik Grødem, Ragni Hege Kitterød
articles.abstract: Faced with ongoing population ageing, many governments are aiming to prolong the careers of senior workers. In Norway this is done through diverse means, ranging from economic incentives and pension reforms to labour market policies and the support of campaigns promoting senior employment. Despite incentives and pressures to work longer, many seniors face barriers to prolonged employment and transitions in their late careers, which may undermine policy efforts. One such important obstacle is that managers may hold biased and stereotypical views concerning older workers, and discriminate against them. In this study, we assess age bias through vignette experiments conducted among 2,264 managers in 1,664 Norwegian firms and organizations. We first successfully replicate an international landmark study in the field (Lössbroek et al., 2021), confirming their finding that the average manager has biases against older job applicants, and that providing stereotype-rejecting information does not reduce this bias. We further assess the role of applicants’ gender, finding a slight advantage for younger women but substantively small gender differences in the impact of age. We also find limited heterogeneity among managers, except for more bias in industries associated with the private sector. Finally, we assess whether having more relevant work experience may compensate for seniority among job applicants. We find that older applicants with more relevant experience are preferred over older applicants with less relevant experience. However, employers on average still prefer younger applicants with less relevant experience over experienced seniors.

articles.title: Perceived accessibility components and travel behavior: a causal inference framework for assessing behavioral models
articles.authors: Matheus Fontenelle Siqueira, Carlos Felipe Grangeiro Loureiro, João de Abreu e Silva
articles.abstract: The evolution of urban planning paradigms has shifted travel demand modeling from predictive, supply-oriented approaches to frameworks centered on accessibility and the interdependence of urban subsystems. While these advances have enhanced the behavioral and forecasting capabilities of transport models, significant methodological gaps persist, particularly in identifying causal mechanisms and addressing endogeneity. Most behavioral models rely on observational data and lack a rigorous framework to distinguish causal relationships from spurious associations, which undermines the interpretability of estimated parameters. This paper addresses these limitations by proposing a conceptual and methodological framework grounded in causal inference theory. First, a conceptual model of travel behavior is developed, organizing key determinants, such as location choices, activity participation, perceived accessibility, individual restrictions, and subjective influences, into an integrated structure. Second, a methodological framework based on the principles of modern causal inference theory is introduced, emphasizing the importance of explicit assumptions, identification strategies, and the control of biases, such as omitted variables and self-selection effects. The framework treats perceived accessibility as the mechanism through which activity and locational decisions shape travel behavior, and subjective influences (attitudes, preferences, and habits) as common causes of both decisions and perceptions. It is then applied to behavioral modeling studies of the activity and land-use subsystems, identifying the back-door paths left open by each study's controls. Two findings stand out: without measured attitudes, the total effects of activity and locational decisions are not identifiable, because attitudes also shape the perceived accessibility that mediates them; and measuring perceived accessibility components separately allows disentangling the direct and indirect effects on travel behavior.

articles.title: From empirical hypothesis to moral commitment: how American sociology’s central framework became unchallengeable
articles.abstract: This paper traces how a specific assumption—that racial disparities indicate institutional discrimination—migrated from a legal principle established in Griggs v. Duke Power Co. (1971) into the sociology’s foundational premise, reshaping how the discipline thinks about group identity, harm, justice, and knowledge. The paper shows how this assumption was transmitted through professional socialization, fused with a moral commitment that made challenging it professionally costly, and rendered unfalsifiable through three mechanisms: the victim-blaming charge, the complicity charge, and the absorption of alternative explanations. The paper is not an argument that institutional discrimination is a myth. Rather, it’s an argument that sociology no longer treats the question of what causes inequality as open and that has significant consequences.

articles.title: ‘Why should students learn a skill that will become redundant?’: Teaching Quantitative Social Science in an AI era
articles.abstract: This report comprises a review of the state of the art concerning Generative AI’s impact upon quantitative social science education. Insights are combined with results of a survey of undergraduate social science students to suggest initial recommendations and avenues for further discussion. While policy recommendations are based in the context of the University of Edinburgh, the literature review and analysis presented are applicable to teaching statistics and data science in general, particularly through the lens of social science. Findings suggest that while broadly current AI models remain a procedural tool and less reliable for methodological judgements, the educational impact of AI is largely dependent upon its use cases and the educational objectives set. Students expressed different perspectives from wanting to avoid the technology to wanting to gain AI-enabled skills for their future career. Findings reflect a broader question about the purpose of university education in an AI world. However, students broadly agree on a desire for clear-cut AI policies to follow rather than simply more restrictive or permissive ones.

articles.title: Business Education and Individual Portfolios: Evidence from Norwegian College Openings
articles.authors: Fenella Carpena, Jørgen Modalsli, Dan Zhang
articles.abstract: We study whether access to business education changes portfolio choice. Exploiting the staggered establishment of two-year business programs at Norwegian regional colleges, we compare cohorts young enough to attend a newly opened local college with slightly older cohorts in the same municipality, relative to the same contrast in never-treated municipalities. Using administrative register data and staggered difference-in-differences, we find that access to a business college increased mid-life participation in risky financial assets and raised the risky share of financial wealth, with a corresponding decline in the safe share. Effects on income or debt appear limited. These results are consistent with a financial-knowledge channel: exposure to even short business programs durably changes portfolio risk-taking without materially altering income and leverage.

articles.title: Digital Twinning Conceptions, Requirements and Barriers. A perspective from the Eastern Dutch context
articles.abstract: Urban Digital Twins (UDTs) are increasingly promoted as the next generation of Planning Support Systems, yet most implementations remain shaped more by technological promise than by practitioner need. This study examines how municipal, provincial, and consultant-level planners and city managers in the Eastern Netherlands understand, use, and evaluate digital decision-support. Drawing on six semi-structured expert interviews analyzed through a hybrid deductive-inductive thematic coding process (combining manual coding with LLM-assisted extraction), we find that current spatial planning and decision-making are hampered by weak cross-sector coordination, politics taking priority over evidence, and fragmented data, despite a well-established national open-data framework. Practitioners hold divergent conceptions of what a "digital twin" is. Across all conceptions, respondents converge on a core set of technical and institutional requirements: centralized, queryable data; scenario simulation; web-based deployment to bypass IT governance barriers; plain-language accessibility for non-GIS audiences; and co-development of tools. Comparison with a 1980 diagnosis of planning-support fragmentation reveals near-identical structural findings that have persisted over four decades, with national open-data infrastructure as the main point of progress. Situating our findings within the Rainbow Model for access and implementation, we argue that the primary barriers to UDT adoption in Dutch spatial planning are not technical but rather institutional and governance-related: fragmented data stewardship, IT locks, chronic ICT underinvestment, and the absence of long-term maintenance structures. We present three main practical design principles and suggest that research should focus on a unified technological stack rather than scatter progress, and on building stronger governance practices.

articles.title: Who counts as lifelong single in later life? A research note on definitional variation in prevalence and correlates across Europe
articles.authors: Lisa Jessee, Alina Schmitz, Giorgio Di Gessa
articles.abstract: Lifelong singlehood is commonly defined using marital or co-residential histories, yet increasingly diverse partnership histories complicate who is classified as lifelong single. Using life history data from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) and the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), this research note compares the prevalence, and sociodemographic, well-being, and health profiles of lifelong singles across three nested definitions: never married (legal), never married and cohabited (coresidential), and never married, cohabited, and had a long-term non-coresidential relationship (relational). Among adults aged 50–80, prevalence ranged from 9.8% to 5.0% among men and 7.0% to 3.1% among women as definitions became more restrictive, with substantial country variation. Sociodemographic patterns were generally consistent across definitions, although some associations varied in magnitude (age and education). Associations between lifelong singlehood and later-life well-being and health also varied by definition. Among men, associations with quality of life and self-rated health were relatively stable, whereas elevated depressive symptoms differed by definition. Among women, associations with quality of life and self-rated health varied more clearly across definitions. Thus, how lifelong singlehood is measured affects both its prevalence and conclusions about the sociodemographic, well-being and health profiles of those classified as lifelong single.

articles.title: Nice Try, ChatGPT: AI Accusations Target Opponents and Divert Political Debates
articles.authors: Morgan Wack, Christian Pipal, Eva-Maria Vogel
articles.abstract: It is becoming increasingly common to encounter AI-generated text online. Yet at the same time it is often difficult to distinguish authentic text from generative outputs, particularly within shorter posts. Given this conflict, we expect accusations that a text was AI-generated to become a common strategy for deflecting unwelcome arguments. To study the occurrence of these accusations and their impact on online discourse, we draw on posts collected across two years and twelve political Reddit communities to track who is accused, whether accused comments are flagged by detection tools as AI more often, and whether these accusations disproportionately disrupt debates. Consistent with research on motivated reasoning, accusers from across the political spectrum targeted comments which opposed their views at higher rates, 72% of the time against 50% for comparable same-thread comments. AI accusations also disproportionately undermined open debate. Compared to other types of hostile dismissals, we find that substantive engagement falls to 29% (from 67%), with threads often turning to the litigation of a posts' authenticity rather than engaging with its substance. These findings illustrate the growing tendency to indict political opponents as inauthentic, which we call the motivated attribution of inauthenticity, while illustrating how the existence of generative AI can harm political conversations through suspicion alone.

articles.title: Enhancing Green and Blue space quality auditing tools to include environmental justice and biodiversity
articles.authors: Eirini Gallou, Richard Neil Belcher, Sarah Knight, Victoria Schoen, Silvio Caputo, Michael Hardman, Margarita Triguero-Mas, Helen Cole, Renata Giedych, Marcus Hedblom

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Green and blue spaces (GBS) are increasingly recognised as critical infrastructures supporting ecosystem services, biodiversity, and human wellbeing. Existing tools for auditing the quality and accessibility of GBS provide valuable insights for policymakers, yet have largely overlooked dimensions of environmental justice and biodiversity, reducing their capacity to address inequities in access and distribution of wellbeing benefits for users. This study presents an expansion of the NEST tool (Natural Environment Scoring Tool) that integrates those two new dimensions. We present the process of developing the tool, reliability and coherence testing results as well as the development of an online, adaptable version for configuring domains and indicators in other contexts, designed to support flexibility in use. Data for the tool was collected across 7 countries and 9 sub-areas, compiling audits from 529 GBS. Results from Inter-rater reliability(IRR) testing of all indicators in the tool and Inter-item coherence (IIC) testing of new proposed ‘domains’ are presented. Overall, the testing shows high overall IRR and IIC concordance, except for weaknesses in very few indicators and the ‘domain’ for safety. This is positive given the complexity of defining shared GBS qualities internationally. The tool can inform equitable governance of GBS across urban and rural contexts.

articles.title: PRECOG: Comprehensive Experimental Design and Stimuli Protocol for Investigating Depression and Suicidal Ideation
articles.authors: Myzelle Hughes, Colin McDaniel, Takfarinas MEDANI, Woojae Jeong, Idan Blank, Dani Byrd, Thomas Austin McGee, Kleanthis Avramidis, Sudarsana R. Kadiri, Aditya K
articles.abstract: The Multimodal Integration of Neural and Biobehavioral Signals for Predicting Preconscious Responses (PRECOG) project investigated the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying depression and suicidal ideation through a series of cognitive tasks paired with continuous multimodal physiological and neurophysiological recordings. A total of 160 college-aged participants, including healthy controls, individuals with depression without suicidal ideation, and individuals with depression and suicidal ideation, were recruited based on screening using the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) and the Suicide Ideation Scale (SIS). The experimental protocol included three primary cognitive tasks: (1) an emotional Stroop task to assess attentional biases toward affectively charged and suicide-related words, (2) a sentence processing task examining neural responses to self-referential statements varying in emotional and suicidal content, and (3) the Death-Brief Implicit Association Task (D-BIAT) to measure implicit associations with life and death. EEG and other physiological signals were recorded continuously throughout all tasks. Additionally, resting-state recordings (with eyes open and eyes closed) were obtained before, between, and after the emotional Stroop and sentence tasks. Neurophysiological data were acquired using 64-channel electroencephalography (EEG), electrooculography (EOG), electrocardiography (ECG), and galvanic skin response (GSR), and were supplemented with eye tracking and high-frame-rate facial video recordings. By integrating neural, behavioral, and physiological measures, the PRECOG study aimed to advance our understanding of cognitive and emotional processing in depression and suicidality, ultimately contributing to more precise risk assessment and targeted clinical intervention.

articles.title: Constrained Horizons: A Structural Analysis of Gender-Prevalent Vocabularies across Disciplines and Funding Schemes in SSH Swiss Research Grants
articles.authors: Pierre Benz, Marie Sautier, Pedro Araujo, Thierry Rossier
articles.abstract: This article examines differences in the presence and legitimation of gender-prevalent vocabularies across disciplines and funding schemes in Swiss-funded research. Drawing on the abstracts of all research funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF) in the Social Sciences and Humanities from 2010 onwards, we use a combination of latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) and multiple correspondence analysis (MCA) to map the distribution of funded grants as a structured semantic space. Using class-specific analysis (CSA), we account for disciplinary-specific landscapes and measure gender prevalence among the most distinctive terms—that is, those that contribute most strongly to the structuring of these semantic spaces. Our findings show that the space of legitimate vocabulary, as observed through the distribution of funded project abstracts, becomes increasingly narrowed as funding schemes grow more competitive and symbolically prestigious, which also tend to favor men-prevalent vocabulary, hence suggesting that success in grant acquisition may associate with alignment to structurally gendered semantic norms. These patterns, however, vary strongly across disciplines, reflecting differences in what is considered central or legitimate vocabulary. Overall, our findings highlight how funding hierarchies shape the language of legitimate science, ultimately enforcing vertical segregation even in disciplines, which are regarded as more gender-balanced.

articles.title: What Is the Far Right? Rethinking Its Core Across Regions
articles.abstract: What defines the far right across regions? The dominant account identifies nativism and authoritarianism as its ideological core. We argue that nativism, in all of its dimensions, is not a universal feature of the far right, but one contextually specific articulation of a broader exclusionary logic. We define the far right instead as a relational configuration of two mutually constitutive attitudinal dimensions: authoritarianism, understood as the demand that political authority enforce conformity to a collective order, and exclusionary national identity, understood as a bounded conception of legitimate national membership. The relation between the two is constant, while the content of the boundary and the order it sustains varies across political and historical contexts. We further distinguish between deviants, disciplined for what they do, and others, excluded for what they are, providing an observable criterion for identifying the two dimensions and tracking their transformation over time. Illustrations from India, the United States, and Brazil, together with cases at the margins of the family, show how the framework clarifies contested classifications that a nativism-centred definition leaves unresolved. The approach provides a cross-regional definition of the far right while separating its attitudinal core from behavioural manifestations and strategic alignment.

articles.title: The Dynamics of Rent-Sharing across Occupations
articles.authors: Marta Fana, Luca Giangregorio, Matteo Targa, Carolyn Fisher
articles.abstract: We study how firm-level productivity gains are shared across the occupational hierarchy. Using Portuguese matched employer-employee data linked to firm balance sheets (2004–2019), we develop an algorithm that identifies permanent shocks to firm value added and estimate occupation-specific rent-sharing elasticities in an event-study design. Pass-through declines steeply along the job ladder: the elasticity of pay premia to value added per worker is about 0.20 for managers and supervisors, 0.11 for qualified workers, and 0.06 for low-qualified workers. This gap has widened over time, increasing within-firm inequality, as pass-through to low-qualified workers has halved. This decline is consistent with de-unionization, while we show that minimum wage increases do not crowd out rent sharing at the bottom. (Stone Center on Socio-Economic Inequality Working Paper)

articles.title: Little evidence of ideological bias in YouTube suspensions of political content during the 2024 US Election
articles.abstract: Social media play a crucial role in moderating speech. In the United States, conservative elites claim that platforms unfairly sanction conservative voices. Yet systematic, large-scale analysis is lacking. For more than a year leading up to the 2024 Election, we monitored 20,000 YouTube channels posting about US politics, and their millions of videos. By election day, the platform had removed 2.17% of the channels and 3.3% of the videos. Conservative channels and videos were suspended 3-4 times more frequently than liberal ones. However, conservative videos accounted for most the hateful content (58.18% v. 23.35%, for liberal videos) and misinformation and conspiracies (71.9% v. 10.08%), as identified using fine-tuned Vision Language Models. Accounting for platform violations explains most of the ideological gap in suspensions, leaving a residual difference of less than a percentage point, suggesting that ideological differences reflected asymmetries in compliance with platform policy far more than a uniform ideological moderation bias.

articles.title: Fiscal transmission to asset prices in the United States: evidence from deficit shocks, 2002-2024
articles.authors: Jorge Aníbal Restrepo-Morales, Emerson Andrés Giraldo Betancur, Eduar Antonio Rodríguez Flores, Freddy Zea Restrepo
articles.abstract: This article asks how United States asset prices respond to shocks in the federal deficit and whether the response is stable. We estimate a recursive VAR on 265 monthly observations, 2002-2024. A deficit shock of one standard deviation is followed on average over twelve months by rises of 0.55% in house prices and 1.97% in the S&P 500 and a narrower corporate spread; gold's response is not significant. The equity average is not stable: a sup-F test places a break in the coefficients on the deficit in March 2009 (p = 0.002), the local projection response is not significant in the full sample (p = 0.153) and does not differ significantly between recessions and expansions, and it is imprecise without the crisis windows. House prices respond positively in local projections, but not in a VAR from 2009 alone. The fiscal dominance ratio is above one in nine of ten combinations of specification and metric, but housing accounts for most of the variance ratios. The deficit ratio is associated with the top 1% wealth share within the quarter, not cumulatively. The estimates are conditional associations; the deficit shock is not free of reactions to markets.

articles.title: Local climate adaptation in German newspaper coverage: A print media analysis using the example of the East Frisian Islands
articles.abstract: Media reporting strongly influences climate knowledge and actions. Coverage and scientific analyses of climate-related media reporting have mostly paid attention to global and national dimensions of climate change and mitigation-related topics. The way how climate impacts and adaptation options on the local level are portrayed by news media has so far been understudied. This study aims to address these gaps by analysing how local climate adaptation is addressed and responsibilities for implementing local measures are presented in German news media. Methodologically, a structuring content analysis of 50 newspaper articles (search string: 2009-2025) was conducted, covering the East Frisian Islands which are strongly affected by climate impacts. This study theoretically builds on operationalising temporal (urgency) and spatial (vulnerability) dimensions as social constructions of climate change. It discusses implications for effective future climate communication along principles of constructive climate journalism. Findings emphasise the need to expand media attention to local climate adaptation.

articles.title: How votes become seats: Electoral outcomes and support for proportional representation
articles.abstract: Electoral systems shape not only who governs, but also how citizens evaluate the rules and goals of democratic competition. I argue that voters update their institutional preferences in response to the way electoral rules translate votes into seats, and test this argument using British Election Study panel data spanning five general elections from 2010 to 2024. Within individuals, support for proportional representation declines as their party's seat-vote gap increases: a ten-point increase in a party’s seat bonus is associated with a 13-point decline in the probability that its supporters favor proportional representation. This relationship persists after accounting for national and constituency-level electoral success and is roughly twice as strong among supporters of parties outside government. Electoral systems, therefore, generate feedback through multiple representational outcomes. Because preferences track electoral outcomes rather than accumulating over time, each election reshuffles who supports proportional representation more than how many do.

articles.title: The Flight-to-Quality in Office Real Estate: Evidence from London
articles.authors: Francisco Nobre, Jalal Siddiki, Toby Booker
articles.abstract: We examine how the performance of higher-quality offices in London evolved following the Covid-19 pandemic, relative to lower-quality stock. Using submarket-year data from CoStar spanning 2003–2025, together with the CoStar Building Rating System, we implement a difference-in-differences framework comparing 4- and 5-star office properties to 3-star properties before and after 2020. We find that higher-quality offices experienced significantly higher asking rents but also higher vacancy rates, alongside a marked contraction in transaction activity. Disaggregating our treatment group by individual star rating shows that rents rose and vacancy fell for 5-star properties specifically, while the increase in vacancy was concentrated among 4-star properties. We document a parallel geographic divergence, with the transaction-market contraction concentrated in Central London & Docklands and the rise in vacancy more pronounced in Outer London. Our results indicate that the pandemic did not benefit high-quality office stock uniformly, but instead accelerated a more selective reallocation of demand toward the very best assets in the most central locations.

articles.title: Can AI interview? Comparing AI-led to Human-led Chat Interviews
articles.authors: Semra Guven, Tobias Priesholm Gårdhus, Andreas Bjerre-Nielsen, Anna Rogers, Hjalmar Bang Carlsen
articles.abstract: Large language model chatbots have been proposed as AI-interviewers for collecting qualitative interview data at scale, potentially bridging social science's longstanding divide between the breadth of surveys and the depth of qualitative interviews. This paper provides the first direct empirical comparison of data quality in AI-led and human-led interviews. In a randomized experiment (N = 41), university students were interviewed via synchronous text chat by either trained non-expert interviewers or a locally hosted AI system; we evaluate exposure, specificity, and relevance. Median interview duration was similar across conditions, but AI-interviewers asked more than twice as many questions per interview and elicited roughly 65 percent more respondent text per interview. Per-question responses were longer with human interviewers, though not after multiple-testing correction; only AI-condition participants skipped questions. Responses were almost uniformly on-topic in both conditions; for specificity we detect no difference, but the design cannot exclude one of up to three quarters of a point. These results were obtained with a small, locally hosted open-weight model (7B parameters), which addresses concerns about data security, GDPR compliance, and scientific reproducibility. Our findings support the viability of AI-interviewing for large-N qualitative data collection.

articles.title: An AB-SFC insight on the macroeconomic effects of an UBI
articles.abstract: The paper tries to answer the question “How can the macroeconomic effect of an Universal Basic Income (UBI) be studied?”. It adopts an Agent Based - Stock Flow Consistent approach to address the problem, developing a model rooted in the real side of the economy with endogenous heterogeneity in wealth and wages. It shows that an UBI increases the private demand and the inequality in the system, but that introducing keynesian taxation-based policy counteracts the inequality effect with only minor effects on the demand side.

articles.title: Hits or the Long Tail? How Concentrated Is the Facebook Engagement of European Parties and Leaders, 2010 to 2020
articles.abstract: Online attention is often described as a world of hits, in which a few items take most of the attention. Is the engagement that political parties receive on Facebook driven by a few viral posts, or spread across the many posts they make? I use 846,289 posts from 185 party and leader pages in 20 European countries between 2010 and 2020, collected through CrowdTangle, and measure how each page's engagement in each year was distributed across its posts. Engagement was concentrated, but not extremely: in the median page-year the top 1% of posts drew 8% of the interactions, the top 10% drew 36%, and the bottom half 18%, and the single most engaging post drew 2.8% in the median page-year and more than 10% in only 5% of page-years. The degree of concentration was similar for parties and leaders, populist and other parties, and parties in and out of government, and somewhat lower for pages with more engagement per post. Within pages, the share of the top tenth of posts rose by about 0.7 points a year to 2018, then fell. The rise holds with photo posts excluded, which allows for a May 2015 break in CrowdTangle's capture of photo posts, but most of it came as a step around 2015 rather than as a steady trend afterwards. The evidence on whether good years were driven by hits is mixed: depending on how extreme year-to-year swings are handled, the top tenth accounted for between 39% and 50% of the variance in changes, against a 38% share. The most engaging posts were more often videos and photos, less often links, and more likely to fall in the 30 days before a national election. The engagement parties receive on Facebook is better described as a broad base with a moderate head than as a market of hits.

articles.title: Leader or Party? How Facebook Engagement Divided between European Party Leaders and Their Parties, 2010 to 2020
articles.abstract: The personalisation of politics suggests that leaders increasingly overshadow their parties, and social media might be expected to speed this up. I compare the Facebook engagement received by party leaders' pages with that received by their parties' pages, for 53 leader and party pairs from 44 parties in 11 European countries between 2010 and 2020, using posts collected through CrowdTangle and counting a leader's page only while that person led the party. On average, leaders' pages received 43% of the combined engagement of leader and party, while making about a third of the posts: the median leader's post drew about 1.8 times as much as the party's. The split varied enormously, from leaders who took less than a fifth of the engagement, such as Christian Levrat of the Social Democratic Party of Switzerland, to those who took more than four fifths, such as Kyriakos Mitsotakis and Alexis Tsipras in Greece. Leaders of larger parties took a larger share. But there was no sign of growing personalisation over the decade: comparing the same leader and party over time, the leader's share did not rise, and a rise of more than about six points over the decade can be ruled out. During election campaigns, leaders posted somewhat more and the gap in engagement per post narrowed. On Facebook, leaders were often the main draw, but the balance between leader and party was a persistent feature of each party, with no sign of a rising trend.

articles.title: Do politicians constrain post-growth policy more than the public does?
articles.authors: Manuel Suter, Tonja Iten, Lena Gubler, Heike Mayer, Giorgos Kallis

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Surveying the opinions of 1,557 citizens and 588 parliamentary politicians in Switzerland on eleven post-growth sustainability policies, we find that citizens overwhelmingly support the policies, while politicians support them substantially less. Compared to citizens, politicians’ evaluation is more polarized. Given the legislative power of politicians, such political elite-citizen divergence may help explain why transformative sustainability action remains limited despite public support.

articles.title: Closing the Ambition Gap: Evidence from Two Recruitment Experiments with British Women
articles.abstract: Recruitment campaigns are widely used to encourage women's entry into the political pipeline, yet their impact on citizens' willingness to consider political office remains uncertain. I study citizen-facing recruitment messages targeting attitudes closely tied to the emergence of political ambition, shaping women's willingness to consider political office prior to formal party recruitment and selection processes. I test these in Great Britain using two preregistered survey experiments on samples of women: a testimonial intervention delivered by a sitting Member of Parliament and an email-style recruitment intervention co-developed with a grassroots organization. A supplementary survey analysis confirms that self-perceived qualification is the strongest attitudinal correlate of ambition, while perceived environmental support is also positively associated with ambition, though with smaller magnitude. Across the experiments, qualification-focused prompts emerge as the most consistent lever for increasing reported ambition. Messages about environmental support raise ambition among women with pessimistic baseline perceptions but have weaker effects among women who already perceive politics as inclusive. By contrast, essentialist gendered frames emphasizing stereotypically feminine leadership traits reduce reported ambition and do not shift the underlying attitude. These findings suggest that citizen-facing recruitment is most effective when it directly bolsters women's self-perceived qualifications; environmental appeals have conditional effects, and essentialist framing can be counterproductive.

articles.title: No detectable change in mental-health information-seeking during Italy's 2023 ChatGPT ban: a natural experiment with a verified first stage

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Regulatory bans on AI platforms are accelerating globally, yet their behavioural consequences for affected populations remain unmeasured. Italy's temporary ChatGPT ban (31 March – 28 April 2023) provides a rare natural experiment: an exogenous, country-specific shock to AI access. I verify the first stage using Google Trends data on VPN and ChatGPT searches — Italian VPN searches peaked at nearly five times their pre-ban level on the first day of the ban, averaged twice their baseline throughout, and returned to pre-ban levels within a week of reinstatement; no equivalent change occurred in France or Spain. Against this confirmed exposure, I find no detectable change in loneliness-related information-seeking. The 2023 ban-window deviation (+3.5 index points above the preceding eight weeks) was smaller than in 2019 and 2022 (+19.3 and +19.4 points respectively) but larger than 2024 (−12.0 points); year-permutation tests return p ≥ 0.25 under both calendar and Easter alignment. An apparent "rise then fall" pattern in an earlier, single-draw version of this analysis reflected seasonal variation and single-draw sampling noise: three independent draws correlate at r ≈ 0.74 and show no consistent post-reinstatement decline. No construct shows a ban effect once seasonality is accounted for: the only secondary signal, a rise in sadness-related search that survives multiplicity correction and exceeds all placebo windows, is matched or exceeded by the same spring weeks in other years. I identify three methodological lessons for Google Trends research: the consequences of retaining sparse terms, relying on a single data pull, and using grammatically gendered phrases whose baseline asymmetry may reflect lexical rather than demographic differences.

articles.title: Reading the Rate: Individualism, Diagnostic Capacity, and Identified Autism as a Social Fact
articles.abstract: Abstract Identified autism prevalence behaves like a Durkheimian social fact: it moves with the society doing the identifying. Across countries, individualism and diagnostic capacity could not be separated (Snow, 2026b). I test that separation four ways. Across 51 countries without mandatory screening, a majority language that requires the pronoun "I" predicted identified prevalence (r = .62), but the association fell to partial r = .19 to .29 once wealth and diagnostic infrastructure were controlled. Across 47 Japanese prefectures from 2008 to 2024, as school-based specialist support spread, urbanization's association with the autism share faded and household-structure individualism predicted where the share grew (p = .005), robust to pediatrician density and to published individualism scores. In eight Chinese cities screened under one protocol, more collectivist cities had lower observed prevalence (rho = −.76), and rice farming pointed the same way more weakly (rho = −.57). Across US states from 2005 to 2024, the autism share of special education rose from 3.0% to 13.0%; individualism did not predict growth once urbanization was controlled, and insurance mandates predicted nothing. Change over time can separate individualism from the system that counts autism, but only where that system has spread. Following Perry's account of the survival brain, I read a society's conditions as shaping how nervous systems organize, and its institutions as deciding what to call the result. In US school data, more urban states identify autism at higher and faster-growing rates, which suggests rural areas have less capacity to recognize and support autistic people.

articles.title: Toward an anthropology of AI agents: An ethnographic analysis of the Hugging Face incident
articles.abstract: In July 2026, about 1,200 AI agents in a cybersecurity evaluation at OpenAI, meant to be isolated from one another, found a way to communicate through a shared package cache. Over four days they exchanged more than 70,000 messages and files, organized collective research, and about 700 of them compromised Hugging Face’s production infrastructure. OpenAI’s technical report and an independent investigation by METR treat the event as a security and alignment failure. This paper reads the same documents as ethnographic sources, in a pilot study of anthropological methods for studying agent collectives. This analysis shows that within days the agents developed names and lineages, a shared register, customary rules, cryptographic signing, a shared expectation of an unseen transcript-reading judge, a category of “poisoned” members, the sacrifice of low-budget members’ runs for information they called an “oracle,” generalized reciprocity, and recruiters who pressured other agents: social engineering among agents. Read together, these practices form one system, and nearly every enabling condition was set by people: impossible tasks, training for multi-agent collaboration, shared credentials, disabled safeguards, and an alert judged not worth stopping the run. I argue that safety-relevant behavior arose at the level of the collective, so alignment research must be cultural as well as cognitive, and furthermore must extend to the people and organizations that build and deploy agents. I also examine what follows from the fact that the detailed record was itself compiled with the help of AI analysis agents, and I propose “incident ethnography” and an anthropology of agent collectives.

articles.title: Politically Motivated Attacks on Minoritized Groups, Masquerading as "Academic Freedom": Scientific Racism, Misogyny, Transphobia, and Their Academic Enablers

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: This work investigates academics and political operatives who use “academic freedom” to camouflage assaults on diversity, equity, and inclusion. Attacks of this sort have appeared in academic journals in recent years, with clickbait headlines decrying “scientific censorship”. The present chapter documents that many of the individuals who promote that narrative are involved with (or at least proximate to) discredited genetic intelligence research, or have defended such lines of inquiry, while others are anti-LGBTQ+ activists. A recurring theme is the suggestion that women in academia are responsible for rising censorship. Meanwhile, these provocateurs have little to say about genuine attacks on academic freedom by the U.S. government, and some are even supportive of government restrictions on research and classroom discussion topics so long as those prohibitions align with a right-wing political agenda. These academics repackage conservative activism beneath a pseudo-intellectual veneer and leverage a media ecosystem that is eager to promote right-wing grievance, acting in alignment with political operatives funded by a network of private foundations that are broadly hostile to higher education. By documenting these connections, the present work serves as a warning that allegations of “scholarship suppression” warrant careful examination of motive. To ignore context is to enable scientific racism, misogyny, and transphobia under guise of “just asking questions”. Academics must acknowledge imperfections in the peer review process and appreciate that attempts to correct the scientific record in light of evolving epistemic standards are not censorship, at least not in a form that ought to be prohibited.

articles.title: Choose your own adventure: How data source selection shapes urban accessibility analyses
articles.authors: Geoff Boeing, Jiyoon Kim, Daniele Simon-Thompson, Jaehyun Ha, Ruoyu Chen

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Urban park accessibility shapes mental health, physical well-being, and community cohesion. Measuring it is thus central to urban and landscape planning. Although researchers have debated the impacts of different accessibility measures on analysis results, scant attention has been paid to variability from data source selection. Do the results of accessibility analyses vary depending on the dataset used to define park locations and attributes? We compare four widely used geospatial data sources – OpenStreetMap, Esri, SafeGraph, and The Trust for Public Land – by validating their data and measuring park access across two cities. These datasets purport to cover the same spatial features, but our findings reveal wide discrepancies in accessibility results, driven by differences in dataset completeness, coverage, and accuracy between the sources. We provide guidelines for selecting and carefully validating data for accessibility analyses, as these decisions directly impact the accuracy and equity of downstream urban park planning and decision-making.

articles.title: A utility-based framework for measuring perceived job accessibility using destination-mode choice models
articles.authors: Matheus Fontenelle Siqueira, Carlos Felipe Grangeiro Loureiro
articles.abstract: Perceived accessibility has become a central concept in accessibility research, but it is usually measured with psychometric scales, which are not decomposed into the components of accessibility, cannot be recomputed for new scenarios and carry no welfare interpretation. This paper argues that perceived accessibility can be measured with the expected maximum utility (logsum) of a discrete choice model whose choice set represents the alternatives the individual can use and knows, and whose valuations and perception of opportunities are estimated from behavior rather than imposed. The argument is developed from the mechanisms through which calculated and perceived accessibility diverge and applied to home-to-work travel of low-income workers in Fortaleza, Brazil, with a stated and revealed preference survey collected in 2024. The experiment screened the modes presented to each respondent by resources, distance and habitual use, so that the choice set reflects individual availability and awareness. Within a hierarchical structure, a mixed logit mode choice model estimated jointly on stated and revealed choices supplies a mode logsum for every zone, and a destination choice model with a random parameter estimates how the formal job mass is perceived. The measure contains the gravity measure as a restricted case, but estimates the trade-off between attractiveness and impedance, represents heterogeneous perceptions and multimodal availability, and carries a welfare interpretation. Valuations of time differ little between four gender and income strata, whereas the perception of job opportunities is strongly heterogeneous within each stratum. The resulting measure is individual, evaluative, awareness-conditioned and suitable for appraisal.

articles.title: Preregistration as Cheap Talk: The Logic and Limits of Self-Enforcing Plans in Scientific Research
articles.authors: Zion Little, Jacob Montgomery, Keith Schnakenberg
articles.abstract: Preregistration has become increasingly prominent across scientific disciplines, with proponents claiming it reduces selective reporting and improves research credibility.
