Yet its logic is puzzling. Researchers face no formal penalty for straying from their stated plans; indeed, deviations are explicitly condoned. Why should simply announcing a plan change behavior? We address this question by modeling preregistration as a form of cheap talk in a model of private experimentation --- a costless, non-binding announcement that nonetheless shapes reviewer expectations and creates informal discipline through rational belief updating. We show that preregistration can be self-enforcing without any third-party oversight since deviations from an announced plan signal that undisclosed tests failed, and reviewers discount results accordingly. Scientists in our model thus voluntarily choose constraining plans since they lower the evidentiary bar for publication. But the very logic that explains the success of preregistration for enhancing researcher credibility makes its downstream consequences ambiguous. The plans scientists optimally choose retain substantial flexibility for selective reporting while still preserving the credibility benefits of preregistration. The result is that preregistration --- when researchers control plan design --- can produce higher false positive rates than an unrestrictive plan. We discuss how better institutional designs --- such as encouraging disclosure of all preregistered results, and ensuring plans are specific enough that such a norm is meaningful --- would more reliably achieve preregistration's intended goals.

articles.title: Feminist Communication on Facebook: Rights Advocacy and Accompaniment. Text Mining of the Surkuna Case
articles.authors: Jackeline Mendoza, Oscar Molina-Bailon, Yuly Marcillo
articles.abstract: This study examined how feminist communication on Facebook connects rights violations, rights, and responses, drawing on 106 posts published in 2025 by Surkuna, an Ecuadorian organization. The analysis combined text mining, co-occurrence networks, and AI-assisted contextual coding. Messages regarding abortion linked autonomy to both overcoming access barriers and rejecting the forced imposition of the practice. Mobilization, consultation, or outreach appeared in 69% of posts containing institutional or regulatory demands, compared to 26% of all other messages. Accompaniment was expressed through offers of advisory services and accounts of support provided. In the case studied, rights advocacy gains meaning by connecting who can decide, who must respond, and what support is offered when violations occur. Ultimately, the findings provide empirical evidence on how autonomy, institutional accountability, and care are articulated within feminist communication.

articles.title: Fundamental Causes of Crime at Places: Assessing Associations Among Neighborhood Types and Crime Rates Using Geodemographics
articles.abstract: The paper discusses the role of contextual approaches in current spatial criminology, with its focus on variables, net-of-effects, and mechanism-identification. The study outlines how contextual approaches to understanding communities, such as geodemographics, have an affinity to modeling multiple, intertwined neighborhood dimensions. Using a specific-purpose geodemographic classification at the block-group level across Delaware (United States) and eight years of incident and arrest data (2010-2017), the paper shows how multidimensional neighborhood classifications are associated with multiple crime outcomes. The study thus shows how an in-depth descriptive approach can provide complementary insights to variable-centered practices in assessing neighborhood effects. Overall, the study highlights the need to consider fundamental causes in addition to proximal causes and echoes calls for upstream interventions to improve public security.

articles.title: Restraint, Combat Roles, and Human-Rights Abuse: Cross-National Evidence on Policing and Militarisation
articles.abstract: This article examines how restraint-oriented and militarised forms of policing relate to human-rights protection. It asks whether the organisational dynamics associated with police violence vary across these two policing models, and whether militarised practices erode restraint-oriented policing from within the same domestic-security system. I argue that militarisation, understood as involving both material coercive capacity and operational transformations through which military logics are introduced into domestic policing, may affect human-rights outcomes by intensifying the conditions associated with police use of force. Empirically, the article combines original cross-national indicators of policing practices in contentious politics with established measures of extrajudicial killings and physical-integrity violations. The analysis uses a global country-year panel covering 2010–2022, with operational policing models restricted to 2017–2022 due to ACLED coverage. The results show that restraint in contentious policing is associated with lower levels of extrajudicial killings and physical-integrity violations, while different forms of militarised policing are associated with higher levels of abuse. The conditional results further show that combat-oriented policing weakens the protective association between restrain policing and physical-integrity outcomes.The article contributes to the literature by distinguishing restraint-oriented policing, material militarisation, and operational police roles as separate dimensions of domestic coercive organisation. In doing so, it challenges the view of restraint and militarisation as simple opposites, showing instead that they may coexist and interact within the same domestic-security system.

articles.title: Biased Provision: Cross-Provider Divergence in How LLMs and Search Engines Supply Evidence on Contested Political Questions
articles.authors: Morgan Wack, Eva-Maria Vogel, Christian Pipal
articles.abstract: Does the evidence generated to answer political questions depend on which large language model (LLM) users query? We introduce "biased provision" to describe this dependence, which can arise where providers differ in how compliant their models are to user requests. Auditing four LLMs, four search engines, and two hybrids across 8,249 responses to 30 claims, we find similar average rates of disconfirming evidence, evidence against the claim asked about, across system types but larger differences among LLMs. All four LLMs answered neutral questions with similar evidence but diverged once users asked for support, whereas search engines narrowed together only after queries included the user's argument. Search engines supplied the least disconfirming evidence under argued requests, a baseline for claims of chatbot sycophancy. As political questions migrate from search engines to chatbots, the evidence users receive will depend less on the tools people use than on which chatbot's answers they prefer.

articles.title: Affective polarisation in CSES Module 6: a replication pipeline and an exploratory test of GenAI occupational exposure
articles.abstract: This note makes the Reiljan Affective Polarization Index (API) available for CSES Module 6 elections and documents the pipeline that produces it. To our knowledge, as of October 2026, no published work reports API values from Module 6. We replicate published API scores to within 0.000002 (about six significant figures) for 12 elections (2007–2017) in ten countries that are covered by Reiljan et al.’s replication data, compute the index for eight Module 6 elections (five with usable occupation codes) held in 2022–24, and link party-level populism codes from PopuList 4.0 through Party Facts and ParlGov identifiers. As a demonstration, we test whether voters in occupations more exposed to generative AI are more or less affectively polarised, using five studies. Exposure is negatively associated with individual-level API (−0.135 per SD, p = .003), but the estimate falls to −0.082 (p = .27) with ISCO major-group fixed effects. The association with voting for populist parties behaves similarly (−3.1 pp, p = .004; −1.4 pp, p = .31 with ISCO major-group fixed effects). The exposure × populist interaction is not distinguishable from zero (p = .13). Only the far-right vote estimate stays below p = .05 with fixed effects, and it does not in the extended sample. We treat these results as a transparent null from an exploratory design, not as evidence of a causal mechanism. Code and aggregate scores are deposited on Zenodo.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence and organizational change: a bibliometric mapping of AI as a tool and as an object of change (2000–2026)
articles.authors: Angelo Leogrande, Mauro Di Molfetta, Valeria Nortarnicola, Maria Giovanna Trotta, Antonio Volpe Plantamura, Gianluca Zaza
articles.abstract: Research on artificial intelligence (AI) and organizational change is growing fast but fragmented. Two perspectives coexist: one uses AI, defined here as machine learning, natural language processing, generative AI and related intelligent systems, as a tool to diagnose, design, implement and monitor change; the other studies AI as the object whose adoption triggers change. We map the field and how the two perspectives relate. Of 1,402 Scopus records, a large language model applying a criterion calibrated on the author's judgment retained 525 documents (2000–2026). We combined performance analysis, co-citation, bibliographic coupling, keyword and topic analysis, and a coding of change phases. The field has grown by almost 70% a year since 2018, mostly through research on AI as an object; the share of studies using AI as a tool fell from 28% up to 2020 to 11% in 2024–2026. The two perspectives rest on largely separate references. Research on AI as an object forms eight research fronts; research on AI as a tool forms none, and almost half of its documents are disconnected from the main coupling network. Only 32 documents propose or evaluate AI as an instrument for managing change. Diagnosis dominates and studies that use AI across several phases of change are rare. These findings hold under alternative inclusion criteria, except the absence of a tool-based front, which reflects the narrow definition of AI adopted. We argue that the field lacks integration and validation rather than new algorithms, and propose an integrative framework with six propositions.

articles.title: From Private Troubles to Public Issues: E-bike Mobility and Shared Space in Shenzhen
articles.authors: YUMING ZHANG, Zehang Yu, YIXIN HUANG
articles.abstract: When does e-bike mobility become a public issue concerning shared urban space? Drawing on the new mobilities paradigm and socio-technical regime theory, we develop the concept of "spatial publicness of mobility practices" through a case-based approach to complexity. We analyse 405 RedNote threads centred on Shenzhen, each comprising an original post, its static images and comments, using two-step qualitative comparative analysis. Socio-technical grounding in the original post, through technical mediation, spatial anchoring, public issue framing or practitioner positioning, is necessary for spatial publicness. Four sufficient configurations show how this grounding combines with situated articulation: a street setting shown without comment, a station entrance framed as a matter of public order, the work of keeping an owned vehicle usable, and commenters' standpoints on rules and enforcement. Much of what becomes public concerns vehicles at rest. The pavement becomes a borrowed mooring for e-bikes through repeated occupation, and its use becomes speakable mainly when something breaks. Where vehicles are privately owned, riders carry the work of joining rules made separately for sale, registration and road use, while the costs of enforcement fall unevenly across the city's labour and housing geography. Social media takes part in this system, making the occupation look ordinary and pooling the practical knowledge needed to settle notices and recover towed vehicles. The study offers a configurational and multimodal reading of how the use of shared space and its public interpretation become interconnected.

articles.title: Equal on Facebook? Engagement and Vote Shares of European Parties, 2010 to 2020
articles.abstract: Does social media level the field between large and small parties, or do the parties that win votes also win attention online? Research on this question, framed as equalisation against normalisation, has mostly studied what parties do online rather than how audiences respond. I compare each party's share of the interactions received by its country's party pages on Facebook with its share of the vote at the last national election, for 107 party pages in 16 European countries from 2010 to 2020 (875 party-years, 431 million interactions, collected through CrowdTangle). Engagement followed votes, but less than proportionally: a party with twice the vote share of another received about 1.7 times the engagement share (elasticity 0.79, SE 0.08), and 0.84 in the year after an election, when vote shares are freshest. This came almost entirely from what each post received rather than from how much parties posted, since small parties posted nearly as much as large ones. Parties with more than a fifth of the vote received a median of about 40% less of the engagement than of the vote, while at the median those with less than a tenth received slightly more. Engagement was about as concentrated across parties as the vote, but on different parties: the largest party by votes received the most engagement in only a quarter of country-years, well below what random variation around a proportional relationship would produce. Populist parties drew more than their vote share and governing parties less. These patterns did not change detectably over the decade. On Facebook, the attention of party audiences was neither simply normalised nor equalised: it was reordered, with the largest parties rarely at the top.

articles.title: 超越“话语悬浮”：中西古今之争的结构性张力与文化主体性的实践重构
articles.abstract: 摘 要：近年来，“中西古今之争”再度成为学界关注的焦点。然而，当前相关论述多陷于宏大叙事的“话语悬浮”，呈现出“高高举起，轻轻放下”的实践困境。本文认为，文化主体性的建构并非单纯的观念辩论或真理竞争，而是一个深刻的制度性实践过程。本文提出一个包含“话语资源供给”“意义框架建构”与“结构性负载传导”的三维分析模型。研究指出，当前宏大叙事之所以难以落地，微观机制在于个体的“认知带宽”被高强度的生存负载所挤占，导致反思性实践停滞；宏观机制在于新旧意义框架的更替未能跨越既有制度惯性的“路径依赖阈值”。破解这一百年难题，必须超越单纯的文本说服，转向三维同步的制度性干预：优先释放结构性负载以重塑反思空间，重构本土化的评价与分类体系，并通过高频、沉浸式的替代性文化实践完成意义系统的实质性累积。 关键词：中西古今之争；文化主体性；认知带宽；制度供给；路径依赖 Beyond "Discursive Suspension": Structural Tensions in the Debate on Chinese-Western and Ancient-Modern Relations and the Practical Reconstruction of Cultural Subjectivity Abstract: In recent years, the debate on "Chinese-Western and Ancient-Modern relations" has regained prominence in academic circles. However, current discourses often fall into "discursive suspension," presenting a practical dilemma of being "raised high but dropped lightly." This paper argues that the construction of cultural subjectivity is not merely a conceptual debate or a competition of truths, but a profound process of institutional practice. We propose a three-dimensional analytical model encompassing "discursive resource supply," "meaning framework construction," and "structural load transmission." The study indicates that the failure of grand narratives to take root is micro-mechanistically due to individuals' "cognitive bandwidth" being squeezed by high-intensity survival loads, leading to a stagnation of reflective practice. Macro-mechanistically, it is because the replacement of old and new meaning frameworks fails to cross the "path dependence threshold" of institutional inertia. To resolve this century-old dilemma, we must transcend mere textual persuasion and shift to three-dimensional, synchronized institutional interventions: prioritizing the release of structural loads to reshape reflective spaces, reconstructing localized evaluation and classification systems, and achieving substantial accumulation of meaning systems through high-frequency, immersive alternative cultural practices. Keywords: Chinese-Western and Ancient-Modern Debate; Cultural Subjectivity; Cognitive Bandwidth; Institutional Supply; Path Dependence

articles.title: A Study of Control on Internal Monologue from Cognitive Neuroscience and Talk Therapy Perspective
articles.abstract: This study investigated the relationship between self-talk, bilingualism, and cognitive control in a task-switching paradigm. Forty-five participants (34 bilingual, 11 monolingual) completed the Self-Talk Scale and a categorization task measuring mixing costs under auditory and visual cue conditions. We conducted independent samples t-tests and mixed-design ANOVAs to assess group differences. Monolingual participants reported significantly higher self-talk in self-reinforcement, self management, and social assessment, while no group differences were observed for self-criticism. Contrary to predictions of a bilingual advantage, bilingual participants did not outperform monolinguals; instead, older bilinguals showed increased mixing costs, suggesting age-related declines in flexibility. Participants with learning difficulties and those reporting substance use also engaged in higher self-talk, particularly in regulatory domains. Performance improved across groups when cues, especially visual ones, were available. These findings suggest that monolinguals may rely more heavily on verbal self-regulation strategies, whereas bilinguals employ alternative approaches. Results challenge the assumption of a general bilingual advantage in cognitive control.

articles.title: High-Speed English Oral Reading for Cognitive Enhancement 2
articles.abstract: This is the original version. The latest version is available at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23534591 This paper presents a novel cognitive training method based on daily high-speed oral reading of English news articles. The method involves reading aloud at double speed or faster for 30 minutes per day. Preliminary self-observations suggest significant improvements in thinking speed, memory, and overall cognitive performance. This low-cost, easily implementable approach may have broad applications in education, language learning, and cognitive health. I initially trained for about an hour daily, but after refining my method, 30 minutes of focused practice proved equally effective, making the routine both easier and more sustainable. Related Work Previous research has explored several approaches to enhancing cognitive and linguistic performance through reading-based interventions. One well-established line of work is repeated reading fluency training, which has been shown to improve reading speed and comprehension primarily among children and second-language learners [Samuels, 1979]. Another relevant strand involves time-compressed speech, where listeners are exposed to accelerated audio recordings; studies indicate that comprehension can be maintained up to certain compression thresholds, and that exposure can foster auditory adaptation and faster information processing [Foulke & Sticht, 1969; Dupoux & Green, 1997]. These methods, however, typically focus either on passive listening or text repetition, and their primary outcomes concern reading fluency or auditory comprehension. By contrast, the present method emphasizes high-speed oral reading, which requires active articulation at near-limit pacing. This approach simultaneously engages phonological processing, working memory, and motor planning, potentially leading to broader cross-domain cognitive benefits beyond reading fluency alone. To our knowledge, no prior work has directly investigated high-speed oral reading as a systematic training paradigm, making this contribution a novel extension of the existing literature.

articles.title: AI Use in Swiss Public Administration: Lessons for Policymakers
articles.authors: Philipp Trein, Martino Maggetti, Katharina Müller, Lukas Baschung

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: This policy brief presents findings from the Swiss component of a global survey on AI in the public sector (2025–26), based on 411 responses from public employees. It shows frequent use of chatbots and AI assistants, perceptions of risk and opportunity that often coexist, and similar views at federal and cantonal levels. It sets out seven recommendations for governing everyday AI use in Swiss public administration.

articles.title: Office, Rank, and Mobility: Decomposing Historical Chinese Bureaucratic Titles with Language Models
articles.authors: Yue Yu, Jun Chen, Michael Yan Hon Chung, Cameron Campbell
articles.abstract: We introduce a procedure that employs an adapted small language model to decompose compound job titles in bureaucracies and other large organizations into substantively meaningful components using a schema grounded in institutional context. This addresses an issue commonly encountered in historical sources for China and neighboring countries according to which recorded job titles include diverse additional attributes beyond the post, such as location, eligibility, temporary assignments, additional titles, or honors, with no consistent format. This makes it difficult to infer the status of officeholders at scale, because their job titles can’t be matched to a canonical list that also specifies ranks or other measures of status. It may be unclear whether a changed job title reflected a promotion, a demotion, or a lateral transfer. We demonstrate the procedure by applying it to personnel records of 19th century officials in the China Government Employee Database–Qing (CGED-Q) Jinshenlu (JSL). In the Qing bureaucracy, compound titles were common for senior officials and purchased and awarded honors, temporary assignments, and locations were routinely recorded in job titles. The model achieves average agreement with manual annotation of 94 percent across fields, outperforming larger general-purpose models. The model works for job titles written in other scripts: we apply it to the hangul form of the job titles in publicly available career records of Joseon dynasty Korean officials and show that it has high accuracy in identification of departments and posts. Our decomposition thus enables career mobility researchers not only to extract names of posts that can be mapped to administrative rank, but also to separate and make use of other components of job titles relevant to their interests. As a case study, we show that analysis of posts, additional titles, and eligibility extracted from job titles of late Qing officials yields novel insights into dynamics of bureaucratic careers and the composition of officialdom. An analysis of officials from 1830 to 1905 reveals divergent trends after the Taiping Rebellion (1850–1864). While promotion to a higher office within three years declined from 12% to 8%, eligibility for higher office more than tripled, and the share receiving a higher additional title nearly doubled.

articles.title: Ancestral O’Odham Irrigation Design and Implications for Ancient Water Management
articles.abstract: The Ancestral O’Odham, commonly referred to as the Hohokam, engineered and maintained one of the largest preindustrial networks of irrigation canals in the Americas, spanning centuries along the lower Salt River, located in the Phoenix Basin, southern Arizona, USA. This article explores construction and water distribution mechanisms through the design, management, and longevity of those irrigation systems. Despite their vast and complex infrastructure, Ancestral O’Odham irrigation was situated in a society lacking powerful hierarchical elites or a centralized state bureaucracy. Disentangling irrigation control from sociopolitical ownership allows this study to identify managerial mechanisms preserved within the lower Salt River archaeological record.

articles.title: Postpartum Pain Experiences: An Exploratory Study
articles.abstract: Despite growing calls to address the ‘gender pain gap’, postpartum pain remains conspicuously absent from both clinical and lay literature. This dissertation asks how women experience and manage postpartum pain. Drawing on qualitative description and hermeneutic phenomenology, it is based on twelve semi-structured interviews with recent mothers and professionals working on postpartum. Four themes emerged: inadequate conceptualisation, medical neglect, alternative sources of information and the normalisation of pain. Read through feminist and disability studies, neuromatrix theory and Mol’s ‘Logic of Care’, the analysis identifies three mechanisms that obscure postpartum pain: naturalisation, maternal deprioritisation and liminality, both temporal and corporeal. This obscuration has critical hermeneutic implications. It reproduces normative temporality, leaves pain untreated and leaves women without the resources to articulate unfamiliar sensations. As a result, the body comes to be experienced ‘as a stranger’. Untreated pains, read through central sensitisation and ‘neurosignature smudging’, point to the physiological stakes of this estrangement. Finally, the dissertation proposes the Logic of Care as a way forward. It foregrounds shared embodiments, digital ‘care teams’ and an attention to ‘life as task’ that resists the framing of the postpartum as a ‘blip’.

articles.title: 'Multiple Truths, Multiple Experiences’: Assembling the COVID-19 Pandemic in Relation to Disability
articles.abstract: Drawing on assemblage theory, this dissertation examines how the COVID-19 pandemic in the UK has been assembled in relation to ‘disability’. It responds to Goggin and Ellis’s (2020) call to decipher and push back against the ‘enforcing of normalcy’ during the pandemic. The study is based on an online survey (n=198) and 21 semi-structured interviews, conducted eleven months into the pandemic, with self-identified disabled people, medics, students, people in low-income professions and two experts. Three themes emerged: risk management, normative behaviour and mutability. The analysis yields three insights. First, it identifies two mechanisms through which the assemblage of normalcy is maintained: the de-vulnerabilisation of the ‘normative’ population through the vulnerabilisation of the Other, and structured emotion. Second, it reveals the ambivalent materialisations of escaping normalcy. Disabled participants were both marginalised and included, both more ‘vulnerable’ and better equipped, and they both aligned with and resisted normative valuations. Third, it argues for intersectionality as a contingent analytic. During the pandemic, gender was ‘submerged’ as a risk category while ‘race’ and ability were brought into topological proximity. The ‘multiple truths, multiple experiences’ of the pandemic remain structured by affect, and the mutability of ‘disability’ remains ‘wild’.

articles.title: Machine Learning for Environmental Event Detection (MLEED): New Data on Human Responses to Climate
articles.authors: Zung-Ru Lin, Erik Wibbels, Jessamine Idalee Vargas Aceves, Iman Dahr, Jeremy Springman, Anna Cabre, Irina Marinov
articles.abstract: While climate data is abundant, systematic data on social and political adaptations to climate remains limited. We introduce the Machine Learning for Environmental Event Detection (MLEED) dataset, which provides monthly data on environmental events and responses across 69 developing countries from 2012 to 2025. MLEED reads more than 130 million news articles from domestic, regional, and international media outlets and uses a fine-tuned large language model to classify each story into 16 types of environmental and adaptation events. We geolocate reports to the country, regional, and district level providing unique data on social and political adaptation over time and space. We describe the corpus, pipeline and data and provide a use case that combines MLEED with climate, agriculture, and migration data to provide new insight into how environmental stress relates to monthly migration from Central America to the U.S.

articles.title: Convictions and Connections
articles.authors: Joseph Charles Roso, Gabriel Varela, Joseph M Quinn
articles.abstract: What keeps people in groups? Shared values or structural embeddedness? Disentangling these mechanisms is challenging because they are mutually constitutive and often correlated in observational studies. We address this question through a recent case of a normative organization splitting over its formally stated values. Specifically, we use a census survey of leaders in the United Methodist Church (UMC) in North Carolina during its schism over same-sex marriage. We first show that most clergy who opposed same-sex marriage left the UMC, but many remained, showing that values-alignment alone does not explain why clergy stayed in the UMC. Next, we used whole-network data to identify three forms of embeddedness which explain why some clergy stayed despite values-misalignment: formal institutional role, global network position, and local network-alignment. These findings show that macro-level, meso-level, and micro-level forms of structural embeddedness can combine to generate behavioral group commitments amongst members of normative organizations.

articles.title: Proximity to Data Centers Predicts Changes in Voter Turnout, Especially Among Independents
articles.authors: Jeffrey L. Jensen, Daniel Karell, Cole Tanigawa-Lau
articles.abstract: Although data centers have rapidly emerged as a political flashpoint, there is little systematic evidence to date on whether their arrival has electoral consequences. We link the precise locations of data centers in Virginia -- which has the United States' largest concentration of such facilities -- to voters' geocoded residential addresses and validated turnout histories, allowing us to compare individual-level changes in turnout between the state's 2021 and 2025 elections according to voters' proximity to operating data centers. Across two independently assembled measures of data-center openings, voters living near an active facility became more likely to vote in 2025. The estimated increase is approximately 0.4 to 0.6 percentage points among voters living within 2.5 to 5 kilometers of a facility. Estimates remain positive at farther distances, although they become less precise. We also find suggestive evidence that the increase in turnout is most concentrated among non-affiliated registered voters and in some regions with many facilities. These results offer insights for states with high numbers of data centers, like Ohio and Texas, and indicate that data-center development was already influencing political participation before the 2026 midterm elections.

articles.title: Children's Education and Parental Longevity. Causal Evidence From Two English School-Leaving Age Reforms
articles.authors: Joan Madia, Patrick Präg, Christiaan Monden
articles.abstract: Parents of better-educated children are healthier and live longer. Is this a return to education that crosses generational boundaries, or is it the consequence of unobserved shared factors driving both children’s education and parental health? Evidence for a causal effect is scarce and mixed for high-income countries. Using data from the English Longitudinal Study of Aging (ELSA) and two educational reforms that raised the mandatory school-leaving age from age 14 to 15 years in 1947 and from age 15 to 16 years in 1972, we investigate the causal effect of children’s education on parental longevity. We replicate the well-known positive association between children’s education and parental survival. However, using a fuzzy regression discontinuity design, we find no evidence of a causal effect. Results are consistent for mothers and fathers and show no systematic variation by child’s gender or parental socioeconomic background. We discuss the implications of these results for the growing literature on educational spillover effects and the specific English context.

articles.title: The Accountability of Missed Opportunities: Electoral punishments from public infrastructure expansion.

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Can public goods expansion generate electoral backlash against incumbents? Do voters hold incumbents accountable for policies from which they derive no direct benefit? Conventional accountability models suggest that public goods provision rewards incumbents, yet the dynamics through which grievances translate into punishment remain both theoretically underdeveloped and empirically underexplored. This paper explores how infrastructure construction can provoke voter backlash in areas unaffected by new developments. Infrastructure provision has inherent characteristics that create particular scenarios for accountability. The visibility and salience of infrastructure, coupled with its differentiated, non-universal spatial impacts and slow expansion, set the stage for territorial competition across constituencies. When policymakers decide the location of new facilities, non-winners are confronted with a tangible counterfactual: the opportunity to enhance their own situation. The perception of having missed a chance to benefit—rather than material loss per se—is at the core of their grievance and becomes the main motivation to punish the incumbent responsible. Using a novel dataset on hospital construction in Spain (2002–2019) and municipality-level electoral results, I analyze how the allocation of 81 new hospitals affected support for regional incumbents. Compared with regions without hospital expansion, municipalities whose accessibility improved increased their support for the incumbent by 2.14 percentage points, whereas non-impacted municipalities reduced it by 1.85 points. Punishments manifest both as lower turnout (-2.26 pp) and as gains for opposition parties (+0.81 pp). Contrary to expectations, however, these punishments do not vary with prior accessibility. This study provides insights into nuanced electoral dynamics around public goods, emphasizing the critical role of unequal allocations in shaping electoral accountability.

articles.title: Practical Framework for Ranking Data Analysis in Political Science
articles.abstract: The concept of rankings has long been central to politics and political institutions. Despite a long history and resurgent interest in political science, statistical methods for analyzing ranking data remain unfamiliar to most political scientists. In this essay, we show how systematic analyses of political rankings enable researchers to uncover rich information about various political phenomena based on rank orderings that has previously been inaccessible to them. We provide a practical guide to analyzing ranking data, highlight its value for applied research, and discuss key caveats and limitations. To illustrate our framework, we show that many essential questions in the study of ranked-choice voting (RCV) can be answered with data on candidate rankings. Our analysis reveals that partisanship can highly structure electoral competition in RCV, demonstrating how ordinal ballots offer insights that categorical ballots cannot provide.

articles.title: The Labour Market Link: An explanation of Brexit support
articles.abstract: Where can we expect support for populist parties and initiatives to be weakest, and why? We argue support will be weakest in places that have experienced strong growth of employment in high-quality jobs, because such growth has positive spillover effects that shape wider perceptions of the economic status quo and the prevailing ideological climate. We test this proposition in relation to Brexit support at the time of the 2016 EU referendum and in the present day, using Census data to proxy the rate at which highly paid jobs replaced low- and mid-paid jobs in English and Welsh Local Authority Districts 1991–2016, and substantiate it at both the area and the individual-level. High-quality employment growth is a more powerful predictor of Brexit support than alternative local economic indicators and individual-level effects are sizeable. All else being equal, analysis of Understanding Society data shows the probability of Brexit support is only 30% among respondents in places that experienced very strong high-quality employment growth, compared to 55% among those in places with negative growth. These findings have important implications for how left behind places should be defined and for strategies that seek to address political discontent.

articles.title: Bigger Page, Fewer Votes: SYRIZA, New Democracy and Facebook in Greece, 2015 to 2020
articles.abstract: In 2019 New Democracy won a parliamentary majority in Greece with 40% of the vote, ending four and a half years of SYRIZA government. I use 31,532 posts from the Facebook pages of five Greek parties and four of their leaders, from 2015 to 2020, collected through CrowdTangle, to compare engagement with the vote and to follow the two main leaders' pages through the change of government. In the month before the 2019 European and national elections, the pages of SYRIZA and Alexis Tsipras drew 56% and 61% of the interactions on the five parties' party and leader pages, against 33% and 36% of the vote among the same parties. The pages of New Democracy and Kyriakos Mitsotakis drew 25% and 21%, against 46% of the vote. The gap is consistent with differences in audience size and posting volume rather than weaker posts: Tsipras's page had about three times as many likes as Mitsotakis's, the SYRIZA party page posted far more than New Democracy's, and Mitsotakis's posts drew more interactions per page like. Counting Tsipras's page, the SYRIZA side also drew about four-fifths of the two main parties' interactions before both 2015 elections. In both main parties the leader's page drew most of the engagement: between 74% and 90% of the SYRIZA pair each year and between 82% and 96% of the New Democracy pair once Mitsotakis led it. After Mitsotakis became prime minister, his share of the two leaders' interactions returned from 36% in the quarter before the election to between 51% and 64%, similar to his share in 2016. Angry reactions on Tsipras's page fell from 4.2% of reactions while he was prime minister to 1.0% in opposition, but much of the earlier anger came from a few episodes. On Facebook in 2019, the bigger page belonged to the party that lost. Provenance and AI use. The data were exported from CrowdTangle in 2020 for my doctoral research. This paper builds on my doctoral thesis (Hotham 2021). The analysis and writing were completed in 2026. I wrote the text, with drafting and editing assistance from Claude (Anthropic), which also helped prepare the analysis code and review drafts. I checked the analysis and the text and take responsibility for both.

articles.title: AI as Cultural Infrastructure: Cultural Sovereignty and Civilizational Pluralism beyond Algorithmic Homogenization
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is often understood as a tool that can preserve, translate, promote, or hreaten culture. This article argues that AI does not merely circulate cultural content; it becomes he infrastructure through which cultures are made visible, authorized, translated, valued, and enabled-or prevented--from shaping the future. Through training data, model design recommendation systems, content moderation, and platform ownership, AI determines which languages, aesthetics, memories, and knowledge systems attain cultural authority. Cultural homogenization is therefore not simply the spread of similar content; it is the narrowing of the epistemic, linguistic, aesthetic, and institutional conditions through which different civilizations nake meaning and build futures. The article responds to four central questions: Can Al coexist with cultural plurality? Whose values should AI align with? Who controls cultural data anguages, and creative works? And why is cultural preservation alone insufficient? It argues that these questions require more than better representation or ethical guidelines; they require restructuring the data, value systems, ownership, and governance of Al itself. To address this, the article develops a theory of civilizational pluralist AÏ governance. It advances three concepts cultural data sovereignty, affirming community authority over cultural data, consent, provenance ınd benefit-sharing; pluralist value alignment, treating alignment as participatory and context- sensitive rather than the universalization of one moral framework; and polycentric cultura. accountability, requiring shared responsibility among communities, creators, states, platforms, and global institutions. Drawing on the Himalayan and Nepali context as a lived example of inguistic, religious, and cultural plurality, the article shows that small and plural societies car provide a normative imagination for AI governance beyond Western universalism. It concludes that the central question is no longer only "Who may speak?" but "Whose knowledge, language, memory, and creativity become the infrastructure of AI's future?" Civilizational pluralism requires moving beyond preservation toward cultural sovereignty, equitable cultural economies, participatory value alignment, and polycentric AI governance.

articles.title: Beyond the "Standard Patient": Deinstitutionalisation, Relational Care, and the Structural Barriers to Hepatitis C Elimination for People with Serious Mental Illness
articles.authors: Bradley Underhill, Carolyn Holbrook, Alison R. Yung, Carl I. Moller

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Australia’s 2016 introduction of subsidised Direct-Acting Antiviral therapy was celebrated as a biomedical milestone, yet treatment commencements have dropped 84 percent, creating an elimination plateau that disproportionately impacts people living with severe mental illness. Drawing on thirteen oral history interviews with policy architects, researchers, and outreach clinicians, this study examines the structural mechanisms driving this gap. Applying an intersectional policy analysis and historical-institutionalist framework, we show how deinstitutionalisation legacies, state-federal funding divides, and rigid inpatient pharmacy subsidy rules sustain the "Standard Patient" fallacy. Furthermore, attitudinal stigma and diagnostic overshadowing lead clinicians to deprioritise viral clearance in psychiatric settings. We argue that reaching elimination requires moving beyond population-level biomedical targets toward a rights-based model of "relational delivery" anchored by peer outreach workers.

articles.title: The Governance Manifold: A Curvature–Spectrum Framework for the Structural Constraints of Governance Space
articles.authors: Xibo Wu, Jian Qin, Xiangyu Wang
articles.abstract: Social-science research on social space has long concentrated on how space is produced, while the structural constraints that space itself imposes after being produced have received little systematic attention. This paper develops the concept of a governance manifold—governance space equipped with a metric tensor built from institutional density, power gradient, and information connectivity—and analyses the two structures this metric generates: curvature, which governs the stability and mixing rate of the system, and the spectrum, which defines the set of possible behavioural modes. The two are coupled by the Bochner identity into what we term the curvature–spectrum duality. Our methodological stance is explicitly a structural analogy, not an ontological claim that governance space is a Riemannian manifold. We operationalize the metric tensor from empirical materials, use a minimal three-layer example to show how a position-dependent metric attenuates policy signals, and treat China's urban–rural hukou divide as a paradigmatic singularity. We then formulate five core propositions and four falsifiable hypotheses. An agent-based model shows that the urban–rural signal cliff—with its threshold, singularity-like character—emerges from agents' behaviour on the curved space rather than being assumed, and that this result is robust to a one-at-a-time sensitivity analysis. The contribution is a formal syntax that upgrades the analysis of large-scale governance from metaphor to a formalized, falsifiable programme.

articles.title: Door Preparation: Cosmopolitan Nationalism and the Institutional Sorting of International Baccalaureate Holders in Japanese University Admissions
articles.abstract: How does a national system receive a global educational credential? Research on the International Baccalaureate (IB) has studied schools and policy discourse. It has rarely studied the admissions categories that turn the Diploma into access. This article studies that junction in Japan. National policy set a target for IB schools. In January 2025 a ministry consortium listed 82 universities using IB results in admissions. A documentary census of the IB routes these universities report finds five ways of receiving one Diploma. It was coded by a fixed rule and checked by two blind codings of 15 institutions. Three sort holders by where the Diploma was earned, by nationality, or by application period. Sorting follows the receiving category more than prestige. Where the IB sits inside or beside a returnee or foreign-student category, it tends to take on that category's conditions. The same Diploma also enters a second door, as a foreign qualification in selections sorted by nationality. Several universities are now withdrawing explicit categories while keeping their criteria. The article argues that cosmopolitan nationalism is enacted in admissions categories, through receiving-side work it calls door preparation. It also offers a coded dataset for comparison with other systems.

articles.title: Inheritance Receipt and the Transmission of Bequest Motives
articles.abstract: Demographic change has pushed inheritance receipt later in life as the population ages, while declining fertility concentrates inheritances among fewer heirs. While inheritances increase wealth, they also carry cultural and normative meaning that may shape intergenerational exchanges. In this paper, we test how receiving an inheritance affects one’s bequest motives. Given demographic changes, we also examine heterogeneity by age at receipt and number of children. Using event studies and data from the Health and Retirement Study (1994–2018), we show that eight years after receipt, an inheritance raises the self-reported chances of leaving a $10,000 bequest by 2.5 percentage points and giving motives for a $100,000 bequest by 5 percentage points. These effects persist net of wealth and exceed the effects of financial windfalls. Effects on giving motives are similar across ages at receipt, unlike effects on wealth that decline with age. Effects on giving motives are largest for parents with fewer children; because estates are divided equally by legal and normative default, this concentrates inherited norms among fewer heirs. These results suggest that norms shape the patterns and extent of intergenerational wealth transmission and, alongside broader demographic shifts, are increasingly consequential for family inequality.

articles.title: Specification without determinism: Evaluation suites as the primary product artifact in AI-native development
articles.abstract: While the practice of managing products to be delivered by means of large language models is growing rapidly and spreading, increasingly a new practitioner discourse is spreading in the field of product management. The PRD (Product Requirements Document), that for decades has been the core specification artifact of the function, would be replaced by the evaluation suite: a set of test cases scored by the evaluation environment of the product under development, the suite encoding in executable form what acceptable system behavior looks like. This simple statement is now almost a mantra in the practice of managing products, and so far has not been subject of any in-depth conceptual investigation. In the requirements engineering community for machine-learning-enabled systems, the challenges of specifying such systems have been analyzed in great detail, but this does not yet translate into practical artifacts and practices of requirements engineering that would be used by practitioners in industry. This paper attempts to specify in detail what is actually being replaced by the evaluation suite, and what corresponding problems and challenges are not addressed by the new artifact. The study is of a theoretical nature and builds on two streams of literature: requirements engineering for machine-learning-enabled systems, and measurement validity in artificial intelligence evaluation. First, we clarify that the PRD serves three separate purposes: defining requirements, coordinating stakeholders, and facilitating deliberation about product intent. We then argue that only the first of these functions is actually transferred to the evaluation suite. Next, we introduce the concept of specification residue, i.e. the portion of what has been specified that cannot be encoded in an executable form and therefore ends up in the black box of individual judgment. We identify three types of such residue. Finally, we introduce a contingency framework that specifies under which conditions of outcome measurability and process-constraint density eval-primary specification is appropriate. Our results indicate that executable specification may shift but not reduce the need for human product judgment, and, most importantly, that it removes the key artifact through which such judgment was previously recorded and contested.

articles.title: A Critical Realist framework for structural refusal and epistemic stewardship in big Q qualitative inquiry
articles.abstract: Big Q qualitative inquiry faces a critical juncture regarding its epistemic and material foundations as generative artificial intelligence and large language models increasingly permeate the discipline. This synthesis uses applied retroductive schemas to reveal the generative mechanisms driving automated text processing, and executes an immanent critique of accommodative research paradigms, demonstrating that they commit fundamental ontological category errors and semantic slippage by confusing vector-space statistical token proximity with authentic human Verstehen. Drawing on Critical Realist principles, the paper reveals how cloud-based narrative ingestion operating across anormative black boxes induces a flat empirical ontology. It also demonstrates that large language models lack first-person subjective interiority, thought-infused qualia, and second-person relationality, rendering them structurally incapable of qualitative interpretation. It is therefore necessary to advocate for structural refusal of commercial cloud large language model text ingestion, distinguishing substitutational industrial platforms from non extractive, convivial tools. This operates as an essential act of epistemic stewardship, rehumanisation, and participant data sovereignty.

articles.title: How Long Do Stale Quotes Last? Measuring Latency Arbitrage Windows on XAUUSD at Three Retail Brokers
articles.abstract: Latency arbitrage in retail foreign exchange and CFD markets exploits the interval during which a broker's displayed quote lags a faster reference price. Practitioner sources describe this interval with loose ranges such as 50–200 ms, and the peer-reviewed evidence concerns equities at microsecond scales. This paper measures the interval directly. Using tick recordings of XAUUSD from three sessions at three anonymised retail brokers, each paired with a fast reference feed on a single recording clock, we define stale-quote windows by a cross-side gap threshold and measure their duration exactly within the recording. At a 30-point (0.30 USD) threshold the brokers showed 240 to 824 windows per hour, with median durations of 34 to 56 ms; between 22% and 35% of windows closed within 20 ms and between 19% and 31% remained open beyond 100 ms. A simulated order arriving 30 ms after the signal and closed one second later would have captured a mean gross result of +22, +12 and +2 points on displayed quotes, against −9, −12 and −49 points for random entries. The delay at which the mean result reaches zero ranges from about 40 ms to beyond 150 ms, depending mainly on quote update frequency and spread. A second reference feed produced 4.6 times as many windows but almost no edge, showing that window counts are not a measure of opportunity. Results are reproduced on the export of the recording software and compared with its own 210 simulated trades. The data contain displayed quotes only, so all results are gross upper bounds.

articles.title: Unpaid Care Work and Marital Economic Justice in Bangladesh: A Critical Feminist Socio-Legal Review
articles.abstract: The paper examines the gap between the value of unpaid household production as calculated statistically and the treatment of non-monetary marital contributions within the Bangladeshi legal framework. I integrate the feminist political economy framework, studies on bargaining within the family and substantive equality, information derived from official time-use surveys and the doctrine of marriage-related statutes. According to Bangladesh's 2025 Household Production Satellite Account, the value of unpaid household production in 2021 was BDT 6.673 trillion (18.90 percent of conventional GDP) of which women contribute approximately 85.37 percent. While such economy-wide figures highlight reliance on care they cannot be automatically transferred into monetary compensation for separation. The review first separates dower, maintenance, protection from economic abuse and marital property allocation, and then discusses their differing potential to deal with economic disadvantages related to care-giving. The contribution of existing literature in terms of unpaid care work and post-separation protection has been acknowledged; my contribution is to link the valuation evidence with the current family court framework and to test recognition-based approaches against feminist concerns about commodification, gender stereotyping and implementation. I conclude that the economic justice through marital contribution needs a combination of substantive equality, realistic evidentiary standards and care redistribution.

articles.title: A Safe Harbour in a Cut-Throat World? General and Engineering-Specific Primal World Beliefs Among Indian Engineering Undergraduates
articles.abstract: Primal world beliefs (primals), people's most basic beliefs about whether the world is Safe, Enticing and Alive, predict well-being but have rarely been studied in non-Western students or alongside beliefs about a specific domain. A convenience sample of 108 Indian engineering undergraduates (aged 17–25) completed the 18-item Primals Inventory (PI-18) and 18 new, positively keyed engineering-specific items. Relative to published reference values, students saw the world as markedly less Safe (d = −1.06), with the largest deviations on items describing the world as cut-throat and competitive (86.1% agreed) and as bad. Yet they rated engineering as substantially safer than the world (dz = 0.72, 95% CI [0.51, 1.00]); this elevation persisted when only positively keyed general items were compared (dz = 0.50) and was specific to Safe, with negligible differences for Enticing and Alive. General primals explained only 12%–22% of the variance in engineering-specific beliefs. Measurement analyses showed that reverse-keyed PI-18 items formed a method factor, and that the all-positive engineering items were dominated by one general factor and partly contaminated by acquiescence, except for the Safe subscale. Students may treat engineering as a protected pathway within a threatening world, consistent with compensatory-control and effort-justification accounts that require longitudinal testing. Domain-specific primal measures need balanced keying, and PI-18 studies in India should model keying effects.

articles.title: Article 370, Kashmir, and the Politics of Constitutional Integration in India: Consent, Sovereignty, and Judicial Power

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: The Supreme Court of India on 11 December 2023 in a five-member Constitution Bench, unanimously rejected the retention of the special constitutional status of Jammu and Kashmir under Article 370 of the Constitution. This paper attempts to examines the rational of the judgment and its implications on Indian federalism. It provides doctrinal analysis of the three opinions, arranged around three propositions about consent, voice, and deferral, in addition to Critical Discourse Analysis of the ways in which the judgment frames the Union, the former State and its people, in terms of asymmetric federalism, constitutional morality and critical-legal discourse. Four findings emerge. First, the Court held that the dissolution of the Jammu and Kashmir Constituent Assembly in 1957 did not extinguish the President’s power under Article 370(3), and that the Assembly’s recommendation was ratificatory rather than a binding condition. Read through the first proposition, this makes an asymmetric arrangement that depends on a transient consent institution reversible by the Union. Second, the Court held that Article 367 could not be used through CO 272 to amend Article 370, but upheld the outcome on other powers, so that it affirmed fidelity to procedure in principle and relaxed it in practice. Third, the treatment of voice rests on three distinct holdings: (a) consultation with the State legislature under Article 3 is not binding (b) during President’s Rule under Article 356, Parliament could supply the views of the State legislature; and (c) the second proviso to Article 3 was inapplicable after CO 272. Fourth, the Court left open whether a State may be converted into a Union Territory and relied on the Solicitor General’s assurance that statehood would be restored. Elections took place in September–October 2024, but statehood had not been restored by October 2026. The ruling prefers sticking to rules over what is fair under the Constitution, and it depends on the Union's goodwill to keep working. The paper closes with suggestions and a review of the dispute's international side.

articles.title: The Health Minister's Spring: Alain Berset, Covid-19 and Swiss Parties and Politicians on Facebook, 2015 to 2020
articles.abstract: Switzerland is governed by a collegial Federal Council drawn from the main parties, and some of its members run their own Facebook pages. I use 11,126 posts from eleven Swiss pages, those of the SP, FDP and SVP, five party presidents and three federal councillors, from May 2015 to September 2020, collected through CrowdTangle. Before the pandemic the SVP and SP party pages drew most interactions; the three party pages' shares matched their vote closely before the 2019 federal election but not in 2015. In March to May 2020, the page of Alain Berset, the federal councillor responsible for public health, drew 50% of all interactions on these pages, up from 13% in the previous twelve months and more than the three party pages combined. His median post drew about 15 times as many interactions as before, though he posted no more often, and his page likes rose from about 20,000 in February to 47,000 in June. By late summer the SVP page was again the most engaged, and in the four weeks before its Limitation initiative was put to the vote in September 2020 it drew 62% of interactions. Across 2015 to 2020, engagement rose far more in the weeks before federal elections than before popular votes, and the rise before votes went with extra posting. With few pages, and no Green or Green Liberal party page, the results describe these pages, not the Swiss party system.

articles.title: Alternative Service Delivery Mechanisms: A Scoping Review
articles.authors: Charles Conteh, Calin Murgu, Paul Horvath, Tia Henstra, Rebecca Van Massenhoven
articles.abstract: This scoping review aims to survey the scholarly literature on alternative service delivery (ASD) mechanisms in public policy and administration discourse and practice. In doing so, the authors seek to understand the extent and type of ASDs deployed by governments. ASDs can take several forms, such as creating innovative arms-length organizations within governments, horizontal integration of service delivery between departments and agencies, vertical integration of service between levels of government, and strategic alliances and partnerships with organizations in the private and non-profit sectors. These non-state organizations deployed through ASD mechanisms typically coexist alongside the conventional bureaucratic machinery of government, with its ministries and departments. The focus of this review is on liberal democratic systems with industrialized economies. We intend to map out the existing literature regarding the types of ASDs, their respective policy domains, and their origin, goals, and scale of activity (national or subnational). The review will also examine whether governments’ uses of ASDs have changed since their popularity at the height of the global new public management (NPM) revolution that swept across the discipline and practice of public administration.
